boundary_rationale: Opens on the book's temporal-dynastic frame 'After the death of Saul' (oshb:2Sam.1.1 ויהי אחרי מות שאול), locating David at Ziklag; the messenger's hinneh-marked arrival at web:2Sam.1.2 launches one continuous interrogation scene whose question-answer turns (1:3, 1:4, 1:5) are turn-markers inside a single audience, closing when the Amalekite's first-person narration ends with the crown-and-bracelet handover at web:2Sam.1.10 — the report the rest of the chapter reacts to.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at 1:5 where David's question narrows to the manner of death — rejected because the named-speaker formula there ('David said to the young man who told him') resets the turn, not the scene: same participants, same location, no movement or discourse-frame change; the campaign turn-marker principle keeps Q&A chains within one audience unit.

boundary_rationale: The wayyiqtol chain pivots from speech to symbolic action: David seizes and tears his clothes (web:2Sam.1.11), and the mourning extends to all his men with a formal grief-triad (mourned, wept, fasted) bounded by the time-marker 'until evening' over a four-member object list (Saul, Jonathan, the people of Yahweh, the house of Israel) at web:2Sam.1.12. The unit is a complete ritual response, closed off before the interrogation formula re-opens at 1:13. The Leningrad scribes leave a samekh space after 1:12 (single-witness) — light agreement, nothing the seam depends on.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Absorbing 1:11-12 into the preceding report scene as its immediate sequel — rejected because 1:11 shifts the acting subject from the messenger to David and the action register from dialogue to ritual gesture; the grief-triad plus 'until evening' gives this notice its own internal closure that the audience scene lacks.

boundary_rationale: The interrogation formula 'David said to the young man who told him' (web:2Sam.1.13; oshb וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֗ד אֶל הַנַּ֨עַר֙ הַמַּגִּ֣יד ל֔וֹ) re-opens the hearing after the mourning interlude, and the unit runs a complete judicial arc: identity question (1:13), indictment question invoking 'Yahweh's anointed' (web:2Sam.1.14; מְשִׁ֥יחַ יְהוָֽה), execution order (1:15), and verdict formula 'Your blood be on your head' quoting the man's own confession of slaying 'Yahweh's anointed' (web:2Sam.1.16; מְשִׁ֥יחַ יְהוָֽה again) — an internal keyword repetition of מְשִׁיחַ יְהוָה at 1:14 and 1:16 binding indictment to verdict, though neither instance reaches the span's own opening verse 1:13, so no inclusio is claimed for it. The close instead rests on the tier-1 discourse-frame change at 1:17, where the narration itself shifts into the qinah-introduction formula (וַיְקֹנֵ֣ן דָּוִ֔ד אֶת הַקִּינָ֖ה הַזֹּ֑את). A setumah stands after 1:16 in WLC (single-witness), a faint second voice for a seam the inclusio already carries.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 1:13-16 as a continuation of the 1:1-10 audience since the same parties resume — rejected because the mourning notice interposes a completed ritual scene, and 1:13 restarts with a fresh interrogation formula whose object is now judgment rather than information; merging would flatten the report/verdict two-stage design the chapter builds.

boundary_rationale: A formal lament superscription (web:2Sam.1.17 'David lamented with this lamentation', cognate ויקנן...הקינה at oshb:2Sam.1.17) plus a source citation to the book of Jashar (web:2Sam.1.18) frame the poem; the substrate's q1/q2 poetry markers begin exactly at 1:19. The refrain 'How the mighty have fallen' at web:2Sam.1.19, web:2Sam.1.25, and web:2Sam.1.27 is a tier-1 refrain structure whose final occurrence closes both the poem and the chapter; WLC petuchah after 1:27 (single-witness, parashah-in-Prophets — weak corroboration only) agrees.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the prose header 1:17-18 from the poem 1:19-27 — rejected because the header is the poem's quotation frame (discourse-frame device): 'lamented with this lamentation' is syntactically incomplete without the quoted qinah, and the Jashar citation modifies the song, not the narrative; the campaign keeps quotation frames with their quoted poems.

boundary_rationale: The episode-opening formula 'After this' (ויהי אחרי כן, oshb:2Sam.2.1) launches a divine-inquiry exchange whose four speech-turns (Shall I go up? / Go up / Where? / To Hebron) form one consultation, followed by its narrative execution: the move to Hebron with wives and men (2:2-3) and the anointing of David king over Judah (web:2Sam.2.4), which completes the inquiry's arc — the going-up commanded in 2:1 ends in kingship at Hebron. The closing report 'The men of Jabesh Gilead were those who buried Saul' (2:4b) is the hinge that motivates the next unit's embassy, disclosed here as an in-span trailing notice. That the WLC layout also breaks after 2:4 — a setumah, single-witness — adds only a whisper of support.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the oracle exchange 2:1 from the move-and-anointing 2:2-4 — rejected because the fourfold Q&A is a single consultation (turn-markers, not scene resets) and its imperative 'Go up' is only discharged by the wayyiqtol chain that follows; an inquiry severed from its enacted answer would leave both halves incomplete.

boundary_rationale: The messenger formula 'David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh Gilead' (web:2Sam.2.5) opens a new addressee and communication channel, and the unit is the embassy speech itself: blessing for burying Saul (2:5b-6) pivoting to the overture at 2:7, which opens וְעַתָּ֣ה תֶּחֱזַ֣קְנָה יְדֵיכֶ֗ם — a 3fp jussive/imperfect of חזק whose subject is יְדֵיכֶם ('let your hands be strong') — followed by the verse's actual imperative, וִֽהְיוּ֙ לִבְנֵי חַ֔יִל ('be valiant men'). The address terminates on the anointing declaration, 'the house of Judah have anointed me king over them' (web:2Sam.2.7; וְגַם אֹתִ֗י מָשְׁח֧וּ בֵית יְהוּדָ֛ה לְמֶ֖לֶךְ עֲלֵיהֶֽם), which is what actually ends the unit. An open parashah break (petuchah) follows 2:7 in the Leningrad codex (single-witness); it can lend the seam before Abner's counter-move at 2:8 no more than soft assent.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping 2:5-7 fused to 2:1-4 since the Jabesh report at 2:4b prompts it — rejected because 2:5 opens with a full messenger-dispatch formula to a new, distant addressee (Jabesh Gilead, not Hebron), a tier-1 boundary device; the 2:4b report is the narrative hinge and is disclosed in the prior unit's rationale rather than erasing the formula-marked seam.

boundary_rationale: A disjunctive participant-introduction clause ('Now Abner the son of Ner, captain of Saul's army, had taken Ishbosheth', web:2Sam.2.8; subject-fronted וְאַבְנֵ֣ר בֶּן נֵ֔ר at oshb:2Sam.2.8, waw + fronted subject before the verb לָקַ֗ח) breaks the storyline to open the rival-kingdom thread: transfer to Mahanaim (2:8) and the six-member installation list at 2:9 — הַגִּלְעָד, הָאֲשׁוּרִי, יִזְרְעֶאל, אֶפְרַיִם, בִּנְיָמִן, and the summarizing עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל כֻּלֹּה ('over all Israel') — five named territories plus the totalizing sixth member, not a seven-territory list. The codex opens a fresh section after 2:9 — petuchah, single-witness — though the register change alone decides this edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running 2:8-11 as one unit through the regnal numbers — rejected because 2:10-11 switches register from narrative installation to annalistic accession formula (age at accession, length of reign, rival-duration note), a distinct list/register genre the campaign tags separately (cf. the regnal-notice standard reserved in 1Sam for 13:1).

boundary_rationale: A formal regnal formula: age at accession and reign-length for Ishbosheth (web:2Sam.2.10, 'forty years old… reigned two years') balanced by the disjunctive counter-notice 'But the house of Judah followed David' and David's own Hebron reign-length (web:2Sam.2.11, 'seven years and six months') — the annalistic register (list-formula tier) that steps outside scene time to frame the whole civil-war period. Before Gibeon resumes scene time the WLC also pauses (setumah after 2:11, single-witness), a detail consistent with, but not constitutive of, the boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 2:10-11 to the following Gibeon encounter as its background — rejected because 2:12 re-enters narrated scene time with a movement formula (went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon), while 2:10-11 is durative chronography; the register change, not topic, is the seam.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (contest-at-the-pool battle scene with etiological close)
boundary_rationale: A double movement formula converges the two armies on one location — Abner's force 'went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon' (web:2Sam.2.12) and Joab's force met them at the pool (2:13) — opening a bounded arena scene: the contest proposal exchange (2:14), the numbered pairing 'twelve for Benjamin… twelve of David's servants' (2:15, register-formula), the mutual slaughter with etiological naming Helkath Hazzurim (web:2Sam.2.16), and the day's battle summary with Abner beaten (web:2Sam.2.17), which closes the arena frame.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the unit to 2:23 to include Asahel's pursuit — rejected because 2:18 opens with an existential wayyiqtol participant introduction (web:2Sam.2.18; oshb וַיִּֽהְיוּ שָׁ֗ם שְׁלֹשָׁה֙ בְּנֵ֣י צְרוּיָ֔ה, verb-initial narrative-chain syntax, not disjunctive) followed by a genuinely disjunctive character-note simile (וַעֲשָׂהאֵל֙ קַ֣ל בְּרַגְלָ֔יו כְּאַחַ֥ד הַצְּבָיִ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר בַּשָּׂדֶֽה, 'Asahel was as light of foot as one of the gazelles that are in the field') that re-focuses the narrative from armies to one runner; the etiological naming plus battle summary at 2:16-17 already close the arena scene.

boundary_rationale: The existential wayyiqtol participant introduction 'The three sons of Zeruiah were there' (web:2Sam.2.18; oshb וַיִּֽהְיוּ שָׁ֗ם שְׁלֹשָׁה֙ בְּנֵ֣י צְרוּיָ֔ה, verb-initial narrative-chain syntax) narrows the lens to Asahel via the verse's own genuinely disjunctive character-note (וַעֲשָׂהאֵל֙ קַ֣ל בְּרַגְלָ֔יו כְּאַחַ֥ד הַצְּבָיִ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר בַּשָּׂדֶֽה, the gazelle simile); the vignette runs through Abner's two dissuasion speeches (web:2Sam.2.21, web:2Sam.2.22) to the spear-butt death at web:2Sam.2.23, closing on the crowd-freezing notice 'As many as came to the place… stood still' — a monument-style stop that seals the vignette.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Abner's recognition exchange (2:20-22) from the narration 2:18-19 — rejected because the exchange happens mid-chase between the same two participants with no scene or location shift: the speech-turns are embedded in one continuous pursuit whose only closure is Asahel's fall.

boundary_rationale: The wayyiqtol pursuit clause 'Joab and Abishai pursued Abner' (web:2Sam.2.24; oshb וַֽיִּרְדְּפ֛וּ יוֹאָ֥ב וַאֲבִישַׁ֖י אַחֲרֵ֣י אַבְנֵ֑ר, plain verb-initial narrative syntax with no adversative particle) opens the wider pursuit, and the verse's own genuinely disjunctive circumstantial pair — the sunset time-marker וְהַשֶּׁ֣מֶשׁ בָּ֔אָה and the location fix וְהֵ֗מָּה בָּ֚אוּ עַד גִּבְעַ֣ת אַמָּ֔ה — supplies the tier-1 scene-frame; Benjamin's rally to a hilltop stand (2:25), Abner's sword-devour appeal (web:2Sam.2.26) and Joab's oath-reply (2:27) resolve in the trumpet-halt (web:2Sam.2.28, tier-1 signal-instrument close) and Abner's all-night march back to Mahanaim (2:29). The lexical pairing between the Mahanaim departure at 2:12 (מִֽמַּחֲנַ֖יִם גִּבְעֽוֹנָה) and the return at 2:29 (וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ מַחֲנָֽיִם) is a real cross-unit echo across the whole Gibeon day, but its first member sits in the preceding decision's span (M8-2Sam-009, 2:12-17); it is disclosed here as a thematic day-frame rather than claimed as a boundary-driving inclusio for this span.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting at 2:26 to make the parley its own unit — rejected because the parley happens at the same hilltop stand-off between the already-present parties: no participant or location change occurs until the trumpet disperses the armies; the speech is the stand-off's resolution mechanism, not a new scene. A larger 2:12-2:29 macro-unit spanning the whole Gibeon day was also considered, prompted by the Mahanaim departure/return echo, but declined because 2:18 opens a distinct off-line participant introduction (Asahel) that the campaign treats as its own vignette (M8-2Sam-010).

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (casualty register and burial itinerary close)
boundary_rationale: Joab's counter-movement 'returned from following Abner' (web:2Sam.2.30) opens the settlement of the day: a numeric casualty register on both sides (nineteen plus Asahel vs three hundred sixty, web:2Sam.2.30-31, list-formula), Asahel's burial in the ancestral tomb at Bethlehem (web:2Sam.2.32), and the mirrored all-night march bringing Joab to Hebron at daybreak — the counterpart to Abner's 2:29 night march, closing the chapter's two-army symmetry.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 2:30-32 to the truce unit — rejected because 2:30 shifts from scene-time confrontation to after-action accounting (musters, tallies, burial), a register change; the twin night-march itineraries (2:29 Abner / 2:32 Joab) are parallel closes of separate units, not one continuous scene.

boundary_rationale: A single-verse durative summary steps outside scene time to characterize the whole period between the two houses: 3:1 opens with the wayyiqtol clause 'Now there was long war between Saul's house and David's house' (web:2Sam.3.1; oshb וַתְּהִ֤י הַמִּלְחָמָה֙ אֲרֻכָּ֔ה בֵּ֚ין בֵּ֣ית שָׁא֔וּל וּבֵ֖ין בֵּ֣ית דָּוִ֑ד, verb-initial narrative-chain syntax, not disjunctive), and its durative/summary force rests instead on the genuinely disjunctive antithetic participial pair that follows in the same verse — וְדָוִד֙ הֹלֵ֣ךְ וְחָזֵ֔ק ('David was going and growing stronger') against וּבֵ֥ית שָׁא֖וּל הֹלְכִ֥ים וְדַלִּֽים ('the house of Saul was going and becoming weaker'), each waw + subject + participle, breaking the narrative chain to characterize the period rather than narrate a discrete event — on the model of the campaign's disjunctive-clause narrator-aside standard (Ruth 2:1/4:7). Its self-containment finds a quiet echo in the closed parashah space (setumah) after 3:1, single-witness testimony that carries corroborative weight only.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Heading the Hebron son-list with 3:1 as its narrative frame — rejected because 3:2 changes register entirely (genealogical list formula 'Sons were born to David in Hebron'), and the war summary's antithetic parallelism is a closed rhetorical shape; the durative notice governs the following chapters generally, not the son-list specifically.

boundary_rationale: A formal birth-register: the list opening 'Sons were born to David in Hebron' (web:2Sam.3.2) runs six numbered entries (firstborn Amnon through sixth Ithream, each with mother's name) and closes with the summarizing inclusio 'These were born to David in Hebron' (web:2Sam.3.5) — an exact frame-repetition bracketing the register. Here too the Masoretic page turns: a petuchah follows 3:5 (single-witness), incidental confirmation of what the frame-repetition establishes. Per the list-register rule the six entries form one cumulative unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting per-son entries or pairing the list with 3:1's war notice — rejected because the entries share one uniform formula with no internal register change, and the list's own inclusio (born-in-Hebron, 3:2/3:5) defines both edges independently of the surrounding war narrative.

boundary_rationale: A Wiederaufnahme re-entry — 'While there was war between Saul's house and David's house' (web:2Sam.3.6) resumes 3:1's durative frame after the son-list interlude (resumption = continuity device marking the return, with the disjunctive note 'Abner made himself strong') — and the scene proper runs Ishbosheth's Rizpah accusation (3:7), Abner's furious oath-speech transferring the kingdom (web:2Sam.3.8-10, oath formula 'God do so to Abner and more also'), and closes on Ishbosheth's silenced fear (web:2Sam.3.11). A closed section space after 3:11 (setumah, single-witness) sits in the same place as this seam without being needed by it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Starting the unit at 3:7 (the concubine notice) and reading 3:6 as the son-list's coda — rejected because 3:6 is syntactically a fresh durative frame (ויהי בהיות המלחמה, oshb:2Sam.3.6) resuming 3:1, not a birth-list formula; the resumptive repetition is precisely the device that re-opens narrative after an inserted register.

boundary_rationale: The messenger formula 'Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf' (web:2Sam.3.12) opens a new channel and addressee — the first Abner-David contact — carrying the land-question overture and covenant offer; David's conditional acceptance with the Michal precondition ('you will not see my face unless…', web:2Sam.3.13) completes the exchange. Where the channel switches to Ishbosheth, WLC happens to insert a setumah after 3:13 (single-witness) — congruent, and no more.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running 3:12-16 as one Michal-retrieval unit — rejected because 3:14 opens a second, distinct messenger dispatch to a different addressee ('David sent messengers to Ishbosheth'), a fresh tier-1 formula: the negotiation (Abner channel) and the enforcement (Ishbosheth channel) are two communication events the text itself separates by dispatch formulas.

boundary_rationale: A second messenger-dispatch formula with new addressee — 'David sent messengers to Ishbosheth' demanding Michal by her bride-price warrant (web:2Sam.3.14) — opens the enforcement unit: Ishbosheth's seizure of Michal from Paltiel (3:15) and the pathos-close of the weeping husband following to Bahurim until Abner's double imperative 'Go! Return!' turns him back (web:2Sam.3.16), which ends the retrieval errand.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending through 3:17-19 (Abner's canvassing) — rejected because 3:17 shifts to a different communicative act with new addressees (Abner to the elders of Israel, then Benjamin), while 3:14-16 is a closed errand whose participants (Ishbosheth, Michal, Paltiel) do not carry forward; the Bahurim turn-back is the errand's terminal point.

boundary_rationale: A new communication event — 'Abner had communication with the elders of Israel' (web:2Sam.3.17) — opens the canvass: the persuasion speech quoting Yahweh's saving promise about David (web:2Sam.3.18, embedded divine-word citation 'By the hand of my servant David…'), the parallel address 'in the ears of Benjamin' (3:19a), and the summary that Abner went to report the consensus 'in the ears of David in Hebron' (3:19b), whose arrival the next unit narrates as scene.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the unit into 3:20 (arrival at Hebron) — rejected because 3:19b is a summarizing itinerary notice (all that seemed good to Israel and Benjamin) while 3:20 re-enters scene time with a participant-arrival formula ('Abner came to David to Hebron, and twenty men with him') and a hospitality event; summary-to-scene is the register seam.

boundary_rationale: The arrival formula with numbered retinue 'Abner came to David to Hebron, and twenty men with him' plus the feast notice (web:2Sam.3.20) opens the summit scene; Abner's covenant-gathering pledge ('I will arise and go, and will gather all Israel to my lord the king', web:2Sam.3.21) and David's dismissal close it with the first occurrence of the 'sent him away, and he went in peace' formula — the refrain the murder narrative will replay twice (3:22, 3:23) with mounting irony.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending to 3:22-25 (Joab's return and protest) — rejected because 3:22 pivots on a hinneh-fronted arrival of a new party (David's servants and Joab from the raid) with Abner now absent — an explicit participant change the text underlines by repeating the in-peace refrain about the departed Abner; the feast scene's own closure is the peace-dismissal.

boundary_rationale: A hinneh-fronted participant arrival — 'Behold, David's servants and Joab came from a raid' (web:2Sam.3.22) — replaces Abner with Joab on stage; the report to Joab (3:23) and his accusatory double-question speech to the king — 'What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you; why is it that you have sent him away… and to know your going out and your coming in?' (web:2Sam.3.24-25) — form one confrontation, closed by the spy-accusation of 3:25 that motivates the murder unit. The 'sent him away… gone in peace' refrain at web:2Sam.3.22 and web:2Sam.3.23 binds the unit to the feast scene as its ironic echo, while the arrival formula separates it as its own confrontation scene.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging with 3:26-27 (the murder) — rejected because 3:26 opens with Joab exiting the royal audience ('When Joab had come out from David') and acting through his own messenger dispatch to Sirah — a location-and-channel change from confrontation speech to covert action, with David explicitly excluded ('but David didn't know it').

boundary_rationale: Joab's exit from the audience ('When Joab had come out from David', web:2Sam.3.26) opens the covert unit: an unauthorized messenger recall from the well of Sirah with the narrator's exculpating disjunctive 'but David didn't know it' (3:26b), and the gate-side ambush killing 'for the blood of Asahel his brother' (web:2Sam.3.27) — deed and blood-motive close the two-verse action.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending through David's curse (3:28-29) — rejected because 3:28 opens with a hearing formula ('Afterward, when David heard it') that shifts scene to David's response-space and register from covert deed to public oath; the narrator's Asahel-motive note at 3:27b already closes the murder's causal arc.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (exculpation oath and curse with narrator verdict)
boundary_rationale: The hearing formula 'Afterward, when David heard it' (web:2Sam.3.28) opens David's response: the innocence declaration ('I and my kingdom are guiltless… of the blood of Abner'), the five-member curse-catalogue on Joab's house (web:2Sam.3.29, list-formula malediction), and the narrator's closing causal verdict naming both brothers ('So Joab and Abishai… killed Abner, because he had killed their brother Asahel', web:2Sam.3.30) — a summarizing seal, behind which the codex's open break after 3:30 (petuchah, single-witness) stands as a mild second.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Placing 3:30 with the murder unit (3:26-27) as its epilogue — rejected because 3:30 is the narrator's retrospective verdict sentence ranging over the whole affair (naming Abishai, absent from the deed-scene) and functions as the curse-unit's warrant, sealing David's guiltless claim; severing it would leave the oath-and-curse unit without its narrative counter-signature.

boundary_rationale: The royal mourning command — 'Tear your clothes… mourn in front of Abner' (web:2Sam.3.31; oshb קִרְע֤וּ בִגְדֵיכֶם֙ וְחִגְר֣וּ שַׂקִּ֔ים וְסִפְד֖וּ, an imperative chain) — opens one funeral-day sequence: bier procession, burial at Hebron with communal weeping (3:32), the embedded two-line qinah fragment over Abner framed by 'The king lamented for Abner and said' (web:2Sam.3.33-34, quotation frame + couplet), the people's renewed weeping, and David's sundown fast-oath refusing bread (web:2Sam.3.35, oath formula 'God do so to me…'). The opening edge rests on 3:31's own imperative chain; the time-marker pair at 3:35 ('while it was yet day… until the sun goes down', בְּע֣וֹד הַיּ֑וֹם ... לִפְנֵ֧י בֽוֹא הַשֶּׁ֛מֶשׁ, eleven words apart within that single verse (הַיּוֹם is 3:35's 9th word, לִפְנֵי its 21st)) locates the fast-oath within the burial day and corroborates that the whole sequence is one day, but it is an intra-verse pair at the unit's close, not a frame bracketing 3:31.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Lifting the qinah couplet 3:33-34 as its own poetry decision on the 1:17-27 model — rejected because unlike the Song of the Bow it carries no independent superscription or source citation: its frame is a single in-scene speech formula and the couplet is grammatically embedded in the funeral procession narrative (the people's weeping resumes mid-verse 3:34b); WLC marks a petuchah after 3:32 (single-witness) but a marker-only case cannot drive a split under the addendum, and no tier-1 device separates burial from lament within the one funeral scene.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:2Sam.3.32 (petuchah, single-witness; not treated as driver)

boundary_rationale: The perception pivot 'All the people took notice of it, and it pleased them' (web:2Sam.3.36) turns from the funeral events to their reception: the narrator's exoneration verdict 'all Israel understood that day that it was not of the king' (web:2Sam.3.37; a petuchah follows in WLC, single-witness, adding modest weight), and David's closing servant-address — the prince-fallen eulogy question (3:38) and the self-assessment 'I am weak today, though anointed king… sons of Zeruiah are too hard for me' with its retribution wish (web:2Sam.3.39) — which closes the Abner affair and the chapter (WLC petuchah after 3:39, single-witness, weak corroboration).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 3:36-37 to the funeral unit and starting a new unit at David's speech 3:38 — rejected because 3:36-39 forms one reception-and-verdict movement (people's perception → narrator's verdict → king's verdict) with no participant or scene change at 3:38: the speech formula there addresses the servants already on scene, a turn inside the same closing tableau.

boundary_rationale: The hearing formula 'When Saul's son heard that Abner was dead in Hebron' (web:2Sam.4.1) opens the collapse notice — feeble hands, troubled Israel — followed by the disjunctive introduction of the two captains Baanah and Rechab (web:2Sam.4.2) with the narrator's Beerothite parenthesis running to 'until today' (web:2Sam.4.3, etiological aside; the WLC's closed break after 4:3, single-witness, leans the same way without deciding anything). The unit assembles the assassination's preconditions: the weakened king and the introduced killers.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the captains' introduction 4:2-3 from the reaction 4:1 — rejected because 4:2 opens with a possessive link to the same subject ('Saul's son had two men…') continuing the exposition begun at 4:1: both verses are off-storyline background to the deed, and the true register break is the Mephibosheth parenthesis at 4:4, which changes subject entirely.

boundary_rationale: A self-contained disjunctive narrator parenthesis steps wholly outside the assassination storyline to plant the Mephibosheth backstory: 4:4 opens with a fronted lamed-possessive prepositional phrase — 'Now Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son who was lame in his feet' (web:2Sam.4.4; oshb וְלִיהֽוֹנָתָן֙ בֶּן שָׁא֔וּל בֵּ֖ן נְכֵ֣ה רַגְלָ֑יִם, with וְלִיהוֹנָתָן בֶּן שָׁאוּל fronted before the verb-less existential-possessive clause whose actual grammatical subject is the following בֵּ֖ן נְכֵ֣ה רַגְלָ֑יִם, 'a son lame of feet') — followed by the age, flight, fall, and name notices, on the campaign's single-verse disjunctive-aside standard (Ruth 2:1, 4:7; 1Sam narrator asides). Neither the preceding captains-exposition nor the following house-entry scene involves this subject.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 4:4 into 4:1-3 as more background — rejected because 4:1-3 exposits the killers and their tribal warrant while 4:4 concerns an unrelated Saulide heir whose relevance only materializes in ch 9: the aside is proleptic planting, not assassination-scene background, and its fronted possessive-phrase syntax marks it as its own parenthesis.

boundary_rationale: The movement formula with time-fix — 'The sons of Rimmon… came at about the heat of the day to the house of Ishbosheth' (web:2Sam.4.5) — re-enters scene time for the deed: the wheat-fetching ruse and body-blow (4:6), the doubled account of the bedroom killing and beheading with the all-night Arabah march (4:7), and the trophy presentation speech at Hebron casting the murder as Yahweh's vengeance (web:2Sam.4.8), which closes the assassins' arc at the point of hand-over. David's reply is preceded in the codex by a setumah space at 4:8 (single-witness) — supportive scenery, not structure.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the journey-and-presentation 4:8 from the deed 4:5-7 — rejected because the trophy speech is the deed's intended completion (the head carried through 4:7's night march is delivered in 4:8's speech): one errand from entry to hand-over, while the true seam is the answer formula at 4:9 where David takes over as speaking subject.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (judicial verdict and execution, Ishbosheth case)
boundary_rationale: The answer formula 'David answered Rechab and Baanah… and said to them' (web:2Sam.4.9) opens the verdict: a life-oath ('As Yahweh lives, who has redeemed my soul'), the Ziklag precedent recalled as case law (web:2Sam.4.10 citing the ch 1 execution), the a-fortiori sentence on the 'righteous person in his own house on his bed' (4:11), and the execution-and-display order with the closing burial of Ishbosheth's head 'in Abner's grave in Hebron' (web:2Sam.4.12) — a burial notice that ties off both ch 3 and ch 4 threads. The judicial arc done, WLC closes the section with a petuchah after 4:12 (single-witness) — a scribal amen to a boundary the execution notice itself supplies.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Making 4:12 a separate execution notice — rejected because the wayyiqtol chain of 4:12 directly discharges the sentence pronounced in 4:11 within the same audience scene (same participants, same location, no discourse frame between verdict and execution); the campaign's judicial-arc precedent (1:13-16) keeps sentence and execution together.

boundary_rationale: A mass participant-arrival formula — 'all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron' (web:2Sam.5.1; oshb וַיָּבֹ֜אוּ כָּל שִׁבְטֵ֧י יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל אֶל דָּוִ֖ד חֶבְר֑וֹנָה) — opens the accession scene: the tribes' kinship-and-shepherd speech quoting Yahweh's oracle ('You will be shepherd of my people Israel', web:2Sam.5.2, embedded divine-word citation), and the completed triple close of covenant, kingship, and anointing 'before Yahweh' at web:2Sam.5.3. The petuchah following 5:3 (single-witness; in the Prophets such parashot corroborate weakly at best) happens to fall exactly where the regnal numbers change the register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending through the regnal summary 5:4-5 — rejected because 5:4 switches register from narrated covenant scene to annalistic accession formula (age at accession, total and per-capital reign-lengths), the same register break as 2:10-11; scene and chronography are kept distinct per the campaign's regnal-notice standard. The identical arrival-and-goal formula at 5:1 recurs at 5:3 (וַ֠יָּבֹאוּ כָּל זִקְנֵ֨י יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל אֶל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ חֶבְר֔וֹנָה, 'all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron') with a different subject; this is not a second arrival event but a resumptive specification — the tribes' mass approach and covenant-speech in 5:1-2 focus down to their representative elders formally executing the covenant, kingship, and anointing acts in 5:3, a spotlighting move (body to representative body) the chapter itself performs, not an unaddressed internal seam.

boundary_rationale: A formal regnal formula for David: age at accession and total reign (web:2Sam.5.4 'thirty years old… reigned forty years') with the itemized capital breakdown (Hebron seven years six months over Judah; Jerusalem thirty-three over all Israel and Judah, web:2Sam.5.5) — durative chronography in the annalistic register, stepping outside scene time exactly as its counterpart 2:10-11 did for the divided period; the Hebron figure repeats 2:11 verbatim, binding the two notices as a frame around the civil war.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 5:4-5 as the closing verses of the anointing scene — rejected because the anointing scene's own closure is the triple covenant-kingship-anointing act at 5:3, while 5:4-5 has no scene participants, dialogue, or wayyiqtol chain: it is register-changed summary spanning forty years, not the Hebron assembly.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (conquest of Jerusalem with etiological saying)
boundary_rationale: The movement formula 'The king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites' (web:2Sam.5.6) opens the conquest: the taunt of the blind and lame (5:6b), the stronghold's capture with the renaming notice 'This is David's city' (web:2Sam.5.7), the watercourse saying with its etiological close 'Therefore they say, The blind and the lame can't come into the house' (web:2Sam.5.8), and the settlement-and-building notice (5:9) sealed by the growth summary 'David grew greater and greater, for Yahweh… was with him' (web:2Sam.5.10) — a theological progress-notice close echoing 3:1. One may note, without leaning on it, that a petuchah stands after 5:10 in the single WLC witness.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the residence-and-growth notice 5:9-10 from the conquest 5:6-8 — rejected because 5:9's wayyiqtol chain (lived, called, built) continues the capture's immediate consequence in the same location with the same subject, and the unit's designed close is the growth formula at 5:10; the true register change is the foreign-embassy notice at 5:11 introducing a new sender (Hiram).

boundary_rationale: The messenger formula with a new foreign sender — 'Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David' with cedar, carpenters, and masons building the palace (web:2Sam.5.11) — opens a compact diplomatic notice closed by David's perception statement 'David perceived that Yahweh had established him king over Israel… for his people Israel's sake' (web:2Sam.5.12), an interior-recognition close that caps the whole establishment sequence begun at 5:1. The setumah at 5:12 (single-witness) is a soft-spoken ally for this close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 5:11-12 to the conquest unit as Jerusalem's build-out — rejected because 5:11 changes the acting subject to a foreign king via a dispatch formula (tier-1 device) and the content from conquest to international recognition; the perception verse 5:12 generalizes over the kingdom, not the city works.

boundary_rationale: A birth-register unit opens with the topic-resuming clause 'David took yet more concubines and wives from Jerusalem' (web:2Sam.5.13; oshb וַיִּקַּח֩ דָּוִ֨ד ע֜וֹד פִּֽלַגְשִׁ֤ים וְנָשִׁים֙ מִיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם, a plain verb-initial wayyiqtol carrying no register formula of its own), whose עוד-resumption ('again/yet more') after the Hiram building notice at 5:11-12 marks a return to the family topic first raised at 3:2-5; the list-opening register formula proper — 'These are the names of those who were born to him in Jerusalem' (web:2Sam.5.14; וְאֵ֗לֶּה שְׁמ֛וֹת הַיִּלֹּדִ֥ים ל֖וֹ בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם) — follows one verse later at 5:14, and the eleven-name chain runs through Eliphelet (web:2Sam.5.16). Unlike the true inclusio at 3:2-5, where the register formula sits on the span's own opening verse (3:2 וַיִּוָּלְד֧וּ לְדָוִ֛ד בָּנִ֖ים בְּחֶבְר֑וֹן) and is answered at its close (3:5 אֵ֛לֶּה יֻלְּד֥וּ לְדָוִ֖ד בְּחֶבְרֽוֹן), 5:13's opening edge rests only on the topic-shift/עוד-resumption — a narrower signal than a register formula. After 5:16 the codex opens a new parashah (petuchah, single-witness), coinciding with the register's own tally-close; per the list-register rule the name-chain is one cumulative unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the prose frame 5:13 from the name-list 5:14-16 — rejected because the frame supplies the place and circumstance (Jerusalem, post-Hebron) the list formula depends on, and no tier-1 device separates 5:13 from the list it introduces; but the 3:2-5 precedent is disanalogous specifically on the near edge (there the register formula opens the span itself, here it opens one verse later), so the near edge is priced on the weaker topic-shift signal alone rather than by direct analogy to 3:2, and confidence is set accordingly.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (first Rephaim campaign with oracle and etiology)
boundary_rationale: The hearing formula 'When the Philistines heard that they had anointed David king' (web:2Sam.5.17) opens the first campaign: deployment in the valley of Rephaim (5:18, disjunctive), the inquiry oracle with explicit deliverance answer (web:2Sam.5.19), the victory at Baal Perazim with David's water-breach saying and the etiological naming 'Therefore he called the name of that place Baal Perazim' (web:2Sam.5.20), and the abandoned-idols spoil notice (web:2Sam.5.21) closing the engagement. That WLC also breaks open after 5:21 (petuchah; only this one witness attests it) is congenial rather than probative.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running both Rephaim campaigns 5:17-25 as one unit — rejected because 5:22 opens a formally new engagement with the iterative formula 'The Philistines came up yet again and spread themselves' repeating 5:18's deployment language (a new-round frame), a second inquiry with an opposite oracle ('You shall not go up'), and a different tactic and itinerary; the paired-campaign design depends on the seam between the two inquiries.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (second Rephaim campaign with sign oracle)
boundary_rationale: The iterative re-deployment formula 'The Philistines came up yet again and spread themselves in the valley of Rephaim' (web:2Sam.5.22) opens the second round: the inquiry now answered with a flanking command and the marching-in-the-treetops sign ('When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees', web:2Sam.5.23-24, sign-oracle discourse frame), and the obedience-execution close 'David did so, as Yahweh commanded him' with the Geba-to-Gezer pursuit itinerary (web:2Sam.5.25). The obedience-execution close is followed in the codex by a petuchah at 5:25 (single-witness), the scribal tradition assenting to what the campaign formula already ended.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the sign-oracle 5:23-24 from its execution 5:25 — rejected because the obedience formula 'did so, as Yahweh commanded' is the oracle's discharge within the same engagement (cf. the 2:1 inquiry precedent): command and enactment form one campaign unit, and no participant or scene change intervenes.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (first ark procession with liturgical celebration)
boundary_rationale: An elliptical iterative clause — 'David again gathered together all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand' (web:2Sam.6.1; oshb וַיֹּ֨סֶף ע֥וֹד דָּוִ֛ד אֶת כָּל בָּח֥וּר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים אָֽלֶף) — opens the ark expedition; MT supplies only the hiphil wayyiqtol of יסף ('David again/added…') governing a bare direct object with no complementary verb of mustering or gathering at all (contrast 5:22, where the same יסף idiom carries its own infinitive, וַיֹּסִ֥פוּ ע֛וֹד פְּלִשְׁתִּ֖ים לַֽעֲל֑וֹת, 'the Philistines again went up'), so 'gathered together' is the WEB's supplied gloss. The opening edge rests on the עוד-resumption plus the participant/topic shift (a fresh muster of 'thirty thousand' replacing the departed Philistine-war forces) rather than on a gathering-verb formula. The unit continues with movement from Baale Judah to fetch the ark under its full Name-title 'called by the Name… Yahweh of Armies who sits above the cherubim' (web:2Sam.6.2), the new-cart arrangement with Uzzah and Ahio (6:3-4), and the whole-house celebration with the six-member instrument list (web:2Sam.6.5, register-formula) — procession in full flight before the Nacon interruption.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the unit through the Uzzah incident to 6:11 — rejected because 6:6 opens with an arrival-at-place formula ('When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon') that pivots the narrative from celebratory procession to fatal incident: the location fix plus the reversal of fortune is the scene seam the chapter's structure turns on.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (Perez Uzzah incident and ark diversion)
boundary_rationale: The arrival formula 'When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon' (web:2Sam.6.6) opens the incident: Uzzah's reach and death by the ark (6:6-7), David's anger with the etiological naming 'he called that place Perez Uzzah to this day' (web:2Sam.6.8), the fear-question 'How could Yahweh's ark come to me?' (web:2Sam.6.9), and the diversion into Obed-Edom's house with the three-month blessing notice (web:2Sam.6.10-11) — a complete halt-arc from stroke to stalled custody, whose blessing close baits the resumption at 6:12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the aftermath 6:9-11 from the death 6:6-8 — rejected because 6:9's fear and 6:10's refusal are the same interrupted journey's immediate disposition (the ark stands mid-route and must go somewhere), with no new participants or movement formula until the report at 6:12; stroke, naming, fear, and diversion form one causal chain at one location.

boundary_rationale: The report formula 'King David was told, Yahweh has blessed the house of Obed-Edom… because of God's ark' (web:2Sam.6.12) triggers the resumed procession: the six-paces sacrifice (web:2Sam.6.13), David's whole-strength dance in the linen ephod (web:2Sam.6.14), and the summary bringing-up 'with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet' (web:2Sam.6.15) — the successful counterpart to 6:1-5, now with sacrificial pacing replacing the cart.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending to the arrival and offerings 6:16-19 — rejected because 6:16 breaks the procession's forward line with a disjunctive simultaneity frame ('As Yahweh's ark came into David's city, Michal… looked out through the window'), introducing a new observing participant and the despising-in-heart counter-theme; the entry-and-aftermath is a distinct movement from the road procession.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (ark installation with Michal window notice)
boundary_rationale: The disjunctive simultaneity frame 'As Yahweh's ark came into David's city, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out through the window… and she despised him in her heart' (web:2Sam.6.16) opens the entry movement: tent installation with burnt and peace offerings (web:2Sam.6.17), the blessing in the name of Yahweh of Armies (6:18), and the food distribution closing with the dispersal formula 'So all the people departed, each to his own house' (web:2Sam.6.19) — a public-ceremony close that empties the stage for the private confrontation.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the Michal glance 6:16 into the confrontation unit 6:20-23 — rejected because 6:16 is grammatically a circumstantial clause synchronized with the ark's entry ('As the ark came…'), planted inside the installation scene as its counter-note; the confrontation proper opens at 6:20 with its own movement formula ('Then David returned to bless his household') and Michal's exit to meet him — that formula, not the window glance, is the scene boundary.

boundary_rationale: The return-movement formula 'Then David returned to bless his household' with Michal coming out to meet him (web:2Sam.6.20) opens the private confrontation: her sarcastic honor-speech (6:20b), David's before-Yahweh retort with the chosen-above-your-father barb and the yet-more-undignified vow (web:2Sam.6.21-22), and the narrator's terminal notice 'Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death' (web:2Sam.6.23) — a lifetime-scope closure sealing both scene and Saulide succession theme. Michal's lifetime-scope notice is capped in the manuscript by an open break after 6:23 (petuchah, single-witness) — decorative agreement at a terminal the narrative sealed itself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching the childlessness notice 6:23 as a standalone narrator aside — rejected because the notice is the confrontation's pronounced consequence, bound to the scene by its subject (the same Michal mid-dialogue) and functioning as the exchange's verdict line; unlike 4:4's proleptic parenthesis it introduces no new thread but closes this one.

boundary_rationale: The settled-rest frame 'When the king lived in his house, and Yahweh had given him rest from all his enemies' (web:2Sam.7.1) opens the audience: David's cedar-house-versus-curtains proposal to Nathan (web:2Sam.7.2) and Nathan's unqualified go-ahead 'Go, do all that is in your heart, for Yahweh is with you' (web:2Sam.7.3) — a completed human exchange that the night oracle will overturn. At the revelation formula's threshold the WLC sets a samekh space after 7:3 (single-witness), which may gently underline, but cannot ground, the seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running the proposal into the oracle 7:4-17 as one prophetic episode — rejected because 7:4 opens with the classic word-event formula at a marked time ('That same night, Yahweh's word came to Nathan') — a tier-1 discourse frame changing speaker (Yahweh), addressee (Nathan alone), and mode (vision-word versus court conversation); the reversal depends on the two units being distinct.

boundary_rationale: The word-event formula 'That same night, Yahweh's word came to Nathan, saying' (web:2Sam.7.4) frames the whole dynastic oracle: the house-question and tent-history retrospect (7:5-7), the shepherd-to-prince biography with the double 'Now therefore tell my servant David' dispatch structure (web:2Sam.7.8), the reversal 'Yahweh will make you a house' (web:2Sam.7.11), the offspring-throne-forever promise with father-son adoption formula (7:12-16 closing 'Your throne will be established forever', web:2Sam.7.16), and the delivery notice 'Nathan spoke to David all these words, and according to all this vision' (web:2Sam.7.17) — a report-frame close matching the opening formula. A setumah trails 7:17 in the codex (single-witness): consonant with the delivery-notice close, nothing more.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the oracle at the second dispatch formula 7:8 ('Now therefore tell my servant David') into negative (no-house-for-me) and positive (house-for-you) halves — rejected because both halves sit inside one word-event frame delivered in one night to one recipient, and the delivery notice at 7:17 reports 'all these words' as a single vision; the dispatch repetition is the oracle's internal hinge, not a frame change.

boundary_rationale: The posture-and-place frame 'Then David the king went in and sat before Yahweh; and he said' (web:2Sam.7.18) opens one continuous prayer answering the oracle: the who-am-I humility opening (7:18b), the incomparability praise 'there is no one like you' (web:2Sam.7.22), the Israel-redemption recital (7:23-24), and the petition turn 'Now, Yahweh God, the word that you have spoken… confirm it forever' (web:2Sam.7.25) building to the double blessing-close on 'the house of your servant' (web:2Sam.7.29) — the prayer's own final word echoing the oracle's house-promise. The prayer's last blessing is also where the Leningrad text opens a new parashah (petuchah after 7:29, single-witness) — an agreeable coincidence of scribe and structure.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the prayer at the petition turn 7:25 into praise and petition halves — rejected because the single speech-frame at 7:18 governs the whole utterance with no intervening narrative or new discourse frame: the 'Now' pivots (7:25, 7:28) are rhetorical stages inside one prayer, exactly the internal-turn case the turn-marker principle keeps whole. A WLC setumah after 7:24 (single-witness) is marker-only evidence there and cannot drive a split under the addendum.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:2Sam.7.24 (setumah, single-witness; not treated as driver)

boundary_rationale: The episode-opening formula 'After this' (ויהי אחרי כן, oshb:2Sam.8.1) launches the victory catalogue in annalistic compression: the Philistine subjugation with the bridle-of-the-mother-city seizure (web:2Sam.8.1) and the Moab defeat with the measuring-line execution notice closing on the vassalage refrain 'became servants to David, and brought tribute' (web:2Sam.8.2) — the refrain that will re-close the Damascus entry (8:6), marking these as catalogue entries of one campaign summary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating all of 8:1-14 as one undivided catalogue — rejected because the catalogue itself changes theater and formula: 8:3 opens the Zobah-Aram complex with a named royal opponent and pursuit clause (a fuller entry-form than the compressed 8:1-2 notices), and the two-refrain architecture (tribute-vassalage 8:2/8:6; victory-wherever 8:6/8:14) partitions the chapter into bounded sub-catalogues the seams of which carry real formula changes.

boundary_rationale: A new catalogue entry with named royal opponent — 'David also struck Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his dominion at the River' (web:2Sam.8.3) — governs the Aram complex: captured forces and hamstrung chariot horses (8:4), the Damascus intervention defeated (8:5), garrisons and the double refrain close 'the Syrians became servants to David, and brought tribute. Yahweh gave victory to David wherever he went' (web:2Sam.8.6), and the spoil notices of the gold shields and the bronze of Betah and Berothai (web:2Sam.8.7-8). Before the Hamath response the manuscript also rests — setumah after 8:8, single-witness — a break that shadows the catalogue-entry seam without carrying it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the spoil notices 8:7-8 from the battle entry — rejected because the spoils are enumerated as proceeds of exactly this campaign (the shields 'on the servants of Hadadezer', the bronze from 'cities of Hadadezer') and the catalogue's entry-form runs battle-garrison-refrain-spoils as one formula; the next entry opens with a fresh hearing formula naming a new king (Toi, 8:9).

boundary_rationale: The hearing formula with a new royal subject — 'When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had struck all the army of Hadadezer' (web:2Sam.8.9) — opens the diplomatic entry: Joram's greeting embassy with silver, gold, and bronze vessels (web:2Sam.8.10), David's dedication of these to Yahweh (8:11), and the summarizing six-item dedication catalogue at 8:12 — מֵאֲרָ֤ם וּמִמּוֹאָב֙ וּמִבְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֔וֹן וּמִפְּלִשְׁתִּ֖ים וּמֵֽעֲמָלֵ֑ק וּמִשְּׁלַ֛ל הֲדַדְעֶ֥זֶר, 'of Aram, of Moab, of the Ammonites, of the Philistines, of Amalek, and of the plunder of Hadadezer' — five nations plus Hadadezer's plunder as the summarizing sixth item, not a sixth nation. It is a cumulative list that retrospects the whole catalogue and closes the tribute theme.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the dedication list 8:11-12 to a spoils unit with 8:7-8 — rejected because 8:11's dedication act is syntactically continuous with the Toi embassy ('King David also dedicated these' — the vessels just presented) and the six-item list is its expansion; splitting would sever the demonstrative's antecedent.

boundary_rationale: The reputation formula 'David earned a reputation when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand men of the Syrians in the Valley of Salt' (web:2Sam.8.13, name-making notice) opens the final catalogue entry: the doubled garrison notice throughout all Edom with Edomite vassalage (web:2Sam.8.14), closed by the repeated theological refrain 'Yahweh gave victory to David wherever he went' — an exact inclusio with 8:6 that brackets the southern and northern campaigns and ends the war catalogue.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 8:13-14 into the Zobah-Damascus entry as more Syrian material — rejected because 8:13 opens with a distinct name-making formula and a new theater (Valley of Salt, Edom), and the refrain's verbatim return at 8:14 is a designed catalogue-closing bracket; the intervening Toi embassy (8:9-12) already separates the entries formally.

boundary_rationale: The reign summary 'David reigned over all Israel; and David executed justice and righteousness for all his people' (web:2Sam.8.15) heads the court register: a varied set of appositional and prepositional office-entries, not a fixed formula. Only Joab takes the עַל-construction, 'over the army' (oshb:2Sam.8.16, וְיוֹאָ֥ב בֶּן צְרוּיָ֖ה עַל הַצָּבָ֑א); Jehoshaphat is bare-appositional 'recorder' (מַזְכִּֽיר); Zadok and Ahimelech are bare-appositional כֹּהֲנִ֑ים ('priests', 8:17), with Seraiah 'scribe' (סוֹפֵֽר); and Benaiah's entry at 8:18 is a bare waw-series with no preposition at all in MT — וּבְנָיָ֨הוּ֙ בֶּן יְה֣וֹיָדָ֔ע וְהַכְּרֵתִ֖י וְהַפְּלֵתִ֑י — unlike the parallel register at 20:23, which does supply עַל before the same office (וּבְנָיָה֙ בֶּן יְה֣וֹיָדָ֔ע עַל הכרי [קרי הַכְּרֵתִ֖י] וְעַל הַפְּלֵתִֽי), confirming the 8:18 variation is a genuine MT feature and not a copying accident. 8:18 closes וּבְנֵ֥י דָוִ֖ד כֹּהֲנִ֥ים הָיֽוּ — the same lexeme כֹּהֲנִים used for Zadok/Ahimelech at 8:17 is applied to David's sons, an MT repetition WEB's inconsistent rendering ('priests' at 8:17, 'chief ministers' at 8:18) obscures. The register's own heading clause at 8:15 governs the whole entry regardless of the internal variation, and its close is also the close of the accession-and-consolidation block (chs 5-8). An open parashah division after 8:18 (petuchah, single-witness) coincides with the register's end, closing block and chapter together in the scribal layout as the office-list does in the text.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the justice summary 8:15 from the officer list 8:16-18 — rejected because the register's own formula makes 8:15 its heading (the reign-wide frame under which the offices are enumerated), matching the parallel register at 20:23-26 which likewise opens on the army-wide notice; a heading split would leave the list without its governing clause.

boundary_rationale: David's programmatic question 'Is there yet any who is left of Saul's house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?' (web:2Sam.9.1) opens the episode and its theme-word chesed; the Ziba interrogation follows in Q&A turns — identification (9:2), the kindness-of-God restatement answered by the lame-son disclosure (web:2Sam.9.3), and the location answer 'in the house of Machir… in Lo Debar' (web:2Sam.9.4) — completing the information phase that the retrieval unit acts on. The turns are turn-markers inside one inquiry audience.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running the inquiry into the retrieval 9:5 — rejected because 9:5 opens with a dispatch-and-retrieval formula ('Then King David sent and brought him out') moving the action from the audience chamber to Lo Debar and onward: information-gathering and enacted summons are separated by the sending formula, the same seam-type as 2:4/2:5.

boundary_rationale: The dispatch formula 'Then King David sent and brought him out of the house of Machir' (web:2Sam.9.5) opens the audience proper: Mephibosheth's arrival with full patronymic and obeisance (web:2Sam.9.6), David's fear-not speech granting Saul's land and the perpetual table ('You will eat bread at my table continually', web:2Sam.9.7 — the episode's refrain), and Mephibosheth's dead-dog self-abasement (web:2Sam.9.8) closing the exchange between these two speakers.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending through the Ziba estate instructions 9:9-13 — rejected because 9:9 opens with a new summons formula to a different addressee ('Then the king called to Ziba, Saul's servant') and the content shifts from personal grant to administrative execution; the David-Mephibosheth exchange closes on Mephibosheth's reply, and the king's next speech is to Ziba.

boundary_rationale: The summons formula with changed addressee — 'Then the king called to Ziba, Saul's servant' (web:2Sam.9.9) — opens the settlement: the grant declaration and land-tilling command with the table refrain repeated (web:2Sam.9.10, plus the disjunctive household note of fifteen sons and twenty servants), Ziba's compliance formula (9:11), the Mica and household notices (9:12), and the summarizing close 'So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate continually at the king's table. He was lame in both his feet' (web:2Sam.9.13; וְה֥וּא פִסֵּ֖חַ שְׁתֵּ֥י רַגְלָֽיו) — a final notice whose table clause caps the episode's own refrain (9:7/9:10) and whose lameness clause echoes the 4:4 parenthesis (בֵּ֖ן נְכֵ֣ה רַגְלָ֑יִם) as a long-range lexical link, disclosed here as thematic rather than boundary-driving since the two instances are nine chapters apart and do not bracket this span. The chapter's last notice is trailed in WLC by a petuchah at 9:13 (single-witness; Prophets parashot rank as weak corroboration), which suits the episode's closure.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching the closing notices 9:12-13 as a separate register — rejected because they continue the settlement's wayyiqtol-plus-notice texture (Mica, servants, residence) and the 9:13 summary is the unit's designed closure, echoing both the refrain (9:7/9:10) and the 4:4 aside; no tier-1 formula separates the notices from the Ziba instructions they conclude.

boundary_rationale: The episode-opening formula 'After this' with the Ammonite succession notice (web:2Sam.10.1) launches the embassy episode: David's kindness motive echoing ch 9's chesed theme (web:2Sam.10.2), the princes' suspicion speech (web:2Sam.10.3), Hanun's beard-and-garment humiliation (10:4), and David's Jericho instruction to the shamed envoys (web:2Sam.10.5) — a completed diplomatic incident that supplies the war's cause.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending to the mercenary hire 10:6 — rejected because 10:6 opens with a perception formula on the Ammonite side ('When the children of Ammon saw that they had become odious to David') and shifts from diplomatic incident to war mobilization with a four-party hire register; cause and consequence are formula-separated.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (two-front battle at Rabbah with battle speech)
boundary_rationale: The perception-and-mobilization formula 'When the children of Ammon saw that they had become odious to David, the children of Ammon sent and hired…' with its four-party mercenary register (web:2Sam.10.6) opens the first engagement: Joab's counter-deployment (10:7-8), the two-front array division with Abishai (web:2Sam.10.9-10), Joab's mutual-aid battle speech with its courage formula 'Be courageous, and let's be strong for our people and for the cities of our God' (web:2Sam.10.11-12), the double rout (10:13-14a), and the closing return 'Then Joab returned from the children of Ammon and came to Jerusalem' (web:2Sam.10.14) — an itinerary close ending the campaign season.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Joab's battle speech 10:11-12 as its own unit — rejected because the speech is delivered mid-deployment to Abishai inside the single battle scene (no location or participant-set change: the two brothers are arranging the two fronts the speech coordinates); speech and engagement form one arc from array to rout.

boundary_rationale: The regrouping formula 'When the Syrians saw that they were defeated by Israel, they gathered themselves together' (web:2Sam.10.15) opens the second, escalated engagement: Hadadezer's beyond-the-River muster under Shobach (web:2Sam.10.16), David's own crossing to Helam (web:2Sam.10.17), the rout with Shobach's death (10:18), and the vassal-kings' peace with the closing notice 'So the Syrians were afraid to help the children of Ammon any more' (web:2Sam.10.19) — a theme-closing verdict that detaches Aram from the Ammonite war and sets up the isolated Rabbah siege of ch 11. With Aram detached from Ammon the codex opens a fresh section (petuchah after 10:19, single-witness) — the layout nodding along with the theme-closing verdict.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at David's personal entry 10:17 — rejected because 10:15-16's muster is the same engagement's build-up (the Helam location named at 10:16 is where 10:17's battle happens); the WLC setumah after 10:17 (single-witness) is marker-only evidence at a mid-battle point and cannot drive a split under the addendum.

literature_type_guess: narrator_frame_notice (spring campaign frame with royal absence)
boundary_rationale: A single-verse campaign frame — 'At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab… and they destroyed the children of Ammon and besieged Rabbah. But David stayed at Jerusalem' (web:2Sam.11.1) — whose season formula opens the siege that 12:26-31 will resume and whose closing disjunctive (וְדָוִ֖ד יוֹשֵׁ֥ב בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם, oshb:2Sam.11.1) plants the royal-absence premise of the whole Bathsheba narrative. The verse is the bracket-opener of the war frame around chs 11-12, on the single-verse durative-notice standard of 3:1. A samekh space follows this one-verse frame in the codex (after 11:1, single-witness), light agreement with its closure; the separate 10:19/11:1 opening seam is already and correctly marked by the petuchah after 10:19, disclosed in M8-2Sam-054.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Opening the Bathsheba scene at 11:1 — rejected because 11:2 carries its own scene-opening time-and-place formula ('At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof') while 11:1 ranges over a campaign season and an army abroad: the frame verse's scope is the Rabbah war (resumed by the Wiederaufnahme at 12:26), and its Jerusalem clause is a hinge the narrative exploits, disclosed here rather than dissolved into either unit.

boundary_rationale: The scene-opening time-and-place formula 'At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king's house' (web:2Sam.11.2) begins the transgression arc: the sighting, the inquiry identifying 'Bathsheba… Uriah the Hittite's wife' (web:2Sam.11.3), the taking with the purification parenthesis and her return home (web:2Sam.11.4), and the conception with Bathsheba's two-word message 'I am with child' (web:2Sam.11.5) — the only words she speaks, closing the unit and detonating the plot.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the conception notice 11:5 as its own unit — rejected because 11:5's message is the direct causal close of the 11:4 encounter (conceived → sent → told) within the same participant pair and time-frame; severing announcement from act would break a four-verse causal chain that the narrative's spare style binds tightly.

boundary_rationale: The send-for formula 'David sent to Joab, Send me Uriah the Hittite' (web:2Sam.11.6) opens the cover-up: the war-news small talk and go-down-to-your-house dismissal (11:7-8), the door-sleeping refusal marked by the recurring 'didn't go down to his house' notice (web:2Sam.11.9), the challenge and Uriah's ark-and-tents oath speech (web:2Sam.11.11), the second-day retention and the drunk-making (11:12-13), closing on the third occurrence of the refrain 'but didn't go down to his house' (web:2Sam.11.13) — a threefold-refusal structure the refrain itself brackets.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Uriah's oath speech 11:11 as its own unit — rejected because the speech answers David's question inside one continuing palace audience (same participants, same location across the three days marked only by 'today also' retention), and the unit's architecture is the triple refrain of refusal that spans 11:9-13; a mid-refrain cut would dismember the pattern.

boundary_rationale: The morning time-marker and writing formula — 'In the morning, David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah' (web:2Sam.11.14) — open a discrete document unit: the quoted letter text 'Send Uriah to the forefront of the hottest battle, and retreat from him, that he may be struck and die' (web:2Sam.11.15, embedded epistolary discourse frame). The letter is the plot's pivot-object, carried by its own victim; the unit is the warrant itself, distinct from the palace dialogues before it and the siege execution after it. The letter's dispatch is shadowed by a closed break at 11:15 in WLC (single-witness), corroboration of the mildest kind.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the letter to the execution scene 11:16-17 — rejected because 11:16 opens on Joab's side with a siege-observation frame ('When Joab kept watch on the city') — a change of acting subject, location (Rabbah), and mode (from written command to military execution); the letter unit ends when the document leaves David's hand.

boundary_rationale: The siege-observation frame 'When Joab kept watch on the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew that valiant men were' (web:2Sam.11.16) opens the warrant's execution at Rabbah: the sortie, the fall of some of David's servants, and the terse fulfillment notice 'and Uriah the Hittite died also' (web:2Sam.11.17) — the death that discharges the letter's order and closes the two-verse action.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging with the report-instruction unit 11:18-21 — rejected because 11:18 opens with a messenger-dispatch formula ('Then Joab sent and told David') moving from battlefield action to communication management: the deed and Joab's stage-managed reporting of it are distinct communicative events, the second built on an anticipatory script.

boundary_rationale: The dispatch formula 'Then Joab sent and told David all the things concerning the war; and he commanded the messenger, saying' (web:2Sam.11.18-19) opens Joab's anticipatory script: the imagined royal-anger scenario with its wall-shooting questions, the Abimelech-at-Thebez millstone exemplum (web:2Sam.11.21, embedded citation of the Judges tradition), and the scripted punch-line 'then you shall say, Your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead' — the script closing on the very information the whole apparatus exists to deliver.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running the script into the delivery 11:22-25 — rejected because 11:22 opens with the messenger's journey formula ('So the messenger went, and came and showed David') shifting location to Jerusalem and speaker to the messenger: instruction scene and delivery scene are twin panels the narrative deliberately doubles, and the seam between them is the itinerary verse.

boundary_rationale: The journey formula 'So the messenger went, and came and showed David all that Joab had sent him for' (web:2Sam.11.22) opens the delivery audience: the battle report placing Uriah's death at its climax (web:2Sam.11.24), and David's return-message 'Don't let this thing displease you, for the sword devours one as well as another' with the siege-encouragement close (web:2Sam.11.25) — the cynical proverb answering Joab's script and completing the communication loop opened at 11:18. The response stays in-unit as the audience's closing turn.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching David's response 11:25 as its own unit — rejected because the response is spoken to the same messenger in the same audience as the report it answers (same participants, no scene change): report and reply are one communicative exchange, the sword-devours proverb being its verdict line, not a new scene.

boundary_rationale: The hearing formula on a new subject — 'When Uriah's wife heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she mourned for her husband' (web:2Sam.11.26) — opens the closure notice: the mourning's passage, the taking-home marriage and birth of the son (11:27a), and the narrator's theological verdict 'But the thing that David had done displeased Yahweh' (web:2Sam.11.27) — a clause-final evaluative wayyiqtol, oshb וַיֵּ֧רַע הַדָּבָ֛ר אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂ֥ה דָוִ֖ד בְּעֵינֵ֥י יְהוָֽה, verb-initial narrative-chain syntax whose force comes from clause-final position and from its lexical reversal of David's own words to Joab at 11:25, אַל יֵרַ֤ע בְּעֵינֶ֨יךָ֙ ('do not let it be evil in your eyes') — the chapter's only evaluative sentence, sealing the whole affair and pivoting to Nathan. The verdict sentence is also where the manuscript turns the page: petuchah after 11:27, on the strength of one witness only.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the verdict clause's verses to ch 12's parable unit — rejected because 12:1 opens with a divine-dispatch formula ('Yahweh sent Nathan to David') that begins a new audience scene with a new participant, while 11:26-27 is summary-time narration (mourning period, marriage, birth) whose verdict is the affair's retrospective seal; verdict and consequence are joined across the seam by theme, not by scene.

boundary_rationale: The divine-dispatch formula 'Yahweh sent Nathan to David' (web:2Sam.12.1) opens the audience: the ewe-lamb parable told as a juridical case (two men, one city — through the traveler's theft, web:2Sam.12.1-4), David's burning anger with the death-deserving oath 'As Yahweh lives' and the fourfold-restitution sentence (web:2Sam.12.5-6) — the entrapment complete when the king rules against himself; the unit closes at the sprung trap, before the application formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running through Nathan's application 12:7-12 as one audience — rejected because 'You are the man! This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says' (12:7) is a formal messenger-formula onset shifting the discourse from fictional case to prophetic oracle — a genre change inside the audience that the campaign's discourse-frame standard treats as a boundary; parable-plus-verdict and oracle-plus-sentence are the scene's two designed movements.

boundary_rationale: The identification-and-messenger formula 'You are the man! This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says' (web:2Sam.12.7) opens the oracle: the anointing-and-gift recital (12:7b-8), the double indictment question 'Why have you despised Yahweh's word' naming Uriah's sword and wife (web:2Sam.12.9), the sword-never-departing sentence (web:2Sam.12.10), and the second oracle formula 'This is what Yahweh says: Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house' with the wives-in-the-sun measure-for-measure sentence and its secret-versus-public close (web:2Sam.12.11-12) — one continuous Nathan utterance whose doubled formula marks the sentence's two counts (sword; house), not a new audience. Ahead of David's confession the WLC leaves a samekh interval at 12:12 (single-witness), faint scribal sympathy for the oracle's close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at the second messenger formula 12:11 — rejected because both oracle movements are delivered in one uninterrupted speech to the same addressee with no narrative re-entry between them (no wayyiqtol frame intervenes); the repeated formula functions as the oracle's internal count-divider, the same internal-hinge case as 7:8, and the WLC setumot at 12:10/12:12 (single-witness) are marker-only evidence there.

boundary_rationale: David's confession formula 'I have sinned against Yahweh' (web:2Sam.12.13) pivots the audience from oracle to absolution: Nathan's immediate remission 'Yahweh also has put away your sin. You will not die' (12:13b) with the however-clause transferring the sentence to the child 'the child also who is born to you will surely die' (web:2Sam.12.14) — a complete two-turn exchange of confession, pardon, and substitute sentence, the audience's resolution. The setumah the codex places after 12:13 (single-witness) lands inside the exchange; a spacing mark alone cannot cut a two-turn audience in half.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending through Nathan's departure and the striking 12:15 — rejected because 12:15 pairs the prophet's exit formula ('Then Nathan departed to his house') with the onset of the illness narrative ('Yahweh struck the child…'), a stage-clearing hinge that opens the next arc; the confession exchange itself closes on the pronounced sentence, and the verse-granular tiling assigns the hinge verse to the arc it initiates.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:2Sam.12.13 (setumah, single-witness; not treated as driver)

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (child's illness, death, and David's reversal)
boundary_rationale: The hinge verse 'Then Nathan departed to his house. Yahweh struck the child that Uriah's wife bore to David' (web:2Sam.12.15) clears the stage and opens the illness arc: the seven-day fast on the ground with the elders' failed intervention (web:2Sam.12.16-17), the child's death and the servants' fearful whispering (12:18), David's perception and the is-he-dead exchange (web:2Sam.12.19), the reversal chain — rose, washed, anointed, changed, worshiped, ate (web:2Sam.12.20) — the servants' bewildered question (12:21), and David's who-knows apologia closing 'I will go to him, but he will not return to me' (web:2Sam.12.22-23) — an aphoristic terminus sealing the arc.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the reversal-and-apologia 12:20-23 from the illness 12:15-19 — rejected because the servants' question at 12:21 explicitly binds the two halves ('You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive, but when the child was dead, you rose up and ate') — the unit's meaning is the before/after contrast itself, and no participant or location change intervenes (palace household throughout); the arc's own closure is David's explanatory speech.

boundary_rationale: The comfort-and-approach formula 'David comforted Bathsheba his wife' (web:2Sam.12.24; oshb וַיְנַחֵ֣ם דָּוִ֗ד אֵ֚ת בַּת שֶׁ֣בַע אִשְׁתּ֔וֹ) opens the birth notice with the narrator's first designation of her by the David-wife epithet בַּת שֶׁ֣בַע אִשְׁתּ֔וֹ ('Bathsheba his wife') rather than by the Uriah-linked designation אֵשֶׁת אוּרִיָּה that the narration still uses as late as 12:15 (וַיִּגֹּ֣ף יְהוָ֗ה אֶת הַיֶּ֜לֶד אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָלְדָ֧ה אֵֽשֶׁת אוּרִיָּ֛ה לְדָוִ֖ד, 'Yahweh struck the child that Uriah's wife bore to David') — after, not before, the 11:27 marriage predicate (וַתְּהִי ל֣וֹ לְאִשָּׁ֔ה, 'she became to him for a wife'). The marriage EVENT and the epithet DESIGNATION are thus distinct: 11:27 records the former, and only 12:24 first supplies the latter. The unit continues with Solomon's birth and naming with the divine-favor clause 'Yahweh loved him', and the prophetic counter-naming by Nathan's hand 'he named him Jedidiah, for Yahweh's sake' (web:2Sam.12.25) — a two-verse naming unit whose double name (human and prophetic) is its own closed structure. Between the double naming and the Rabbah resumption the manuscript interposes an open break (petuchah after 12:25, single-witness) — happy agreement, modest force.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the birth to the illness arc as its consolation coda — rejected because 12:24 opens with a fresh approach formula and the narrator's first epithet-designation of Bathsheba as David's wife (contrast the Uriah-linked designation still used at 12:15), and the content pivots from death to dynastic future: the notice inaugurates the Solomon thread rather than closing the child-death arc, whose own terminus is David's 12:23 aphorism.

boundary_rationale: A lexical Wiederaufnahme re-opens the siege frame planted at 11:1: 12:26 opens with the niphal wayyiqtol 'Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and took the royal city' (web:2Sam.12.26; oshb וַיִּלָּ֣חֶם יוֹאָ֔ב בְּרַבַּ֖ת בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֑וֹן וַיִּלְכֹּ֖ד אֶת עִ֥יר הַמְּלוּכָֽה, verb-initial narrative-chain syntax with the subject following, not disjunctive), resuming רַבַּ֖ת בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֑וֹן from the siege notice at 11:1 (וַיָּצֻ֖רוּ עַל רַבָּ֑ה) together with a change of theatre and acting subject across the intervening Bathsheba complex. Joab's summons message with the city-of-waters report and the take-it-yourself warning 'lest I take the city, and it be called by my name' (web:2Sam.12.27-28), David's muster and capture (12:29), the crown-and-plunder notices (web:2Sam.12.30), the labor-levy disposition of the cities (12:31a), and the closing return formula 'Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem' (web:2Sam.12.31) form the itinerary close that ends the Ammonite war frame. The return-to-Jerusalem formula is seconded by the codex's petuchah at 12:31 (single-witness), scribe and itinerary closing together.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Joab's message 12:26-28 from David's conquest 12:29-31 — rejected because the message's explicit purpose clause (gather the people, lest my name be called over it) is discharged immediately by 12:29's muster in one continuous military operation at one location; summons and response form the resumed frame's single closing movement.

boundary_rationale: The episode-opening formula 'After this' (ויהי אחרי כן, oshb:2Sam.13.1) launches the Amnon-Tamar narrative with a triple character exposition — Tamar's beauty and Amnon's love (web:2Sam.13.1), the love-sick impossibility notice (13:2), and the disjunctive introduction of Jonadab 'a very subtle man' (web:2Sam.13.3) — followed by the diagnostic question (13:4) and Jonadab's feign-sickness scheme speech scripting the request verbatim (web:2Sam.13.5), which the next unit enacts.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending through the scheme's enactment 13:6-7 — rejected because 13:6 opens the enactment with its own wayyiqtol chain ('So Amnon lay down and faked being sick') moving from counsel scene to royal sickroom visit: script and performance are separated by the change of scene and addressee (Jonadab-Amnon private exchange versus Amnon-king audience).

boundary_rationale: The enactment formula 'So Amnon lay down and faked being sick' (web:2Sam.13.6) opens the communication pair: Amnon's cake-request to the visiting king (13:6b, performing Jonadab's script with the sister-hand motif) and David's answering dispatch 'Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, Go now to your brother Amnon's house' (web:2Sam.13.7) — request and unwitting royal command form one completed exchange that moves Tamar toward the trap.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging with the house scene 13:8-14 — rejected because 13:8 opens with Tamar's movement formula ('So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house') shifting location and participant-set (the king exits; Tamar enters): the palace exchange and the house scene are distinct stations of the plot, and the dispatch formula's discharge is the seam.

boundary_rationale: Tamar's movement formula 'So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house' (web:2Sam.13.8) opens the house scene: the cake-preparation in his sight (13:8-9a), the clearing of the room 'Have all men leave me' (web:2Sam.13.9), the chamber summons (13:10), the seizure with 'Come, lie with me, my sister' (web:2Sam.13.11), Tamar's formal protest speech — the no-such-thing-in-Israel appeal, the shame-and-fool argument, and the speak-to-the-king alternative (web:2Sam.13.12-13) — and the overpowering at web:2Sam.13.14, the deed that closes the scene's descent.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Tamar's protest 13:12-13 as its own unit — rejected because the protest is spoken mid-assault between the same two participants in the same chamber (the answer to 13:11's demand, overridden by 13:14's 'However, he would not listen'): the three verses form the scene's pivot, not a separate scene, and severing them would break the demand-refusal-force chain.

boundary_rationale: The reversal notice 'Then Amnon hated her with exceedingly great hatred; for the hatred… was greater than the love' (web:2Sam.13.15) pivots the scene into its second movement: the expulsion order 'Arise, be gone!', Tamar's greater-wrong protest (web:2Sam.13.16), the servant-executed ejection with the bolted door (13:17), the narrator's robe parenthesis on virgin princesses' dress (web:2Sam.13.18), and Tamar's public mourning exit — ashes, torn robe, hand on head, crying aloud (web:2Sam.13.19) — which carries her offstage toward Absalom.
