strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping 13:15-19 inside the rape unit as its immediate sequel — rejected because 13:15's hatred-versus-love antithesis is a formal reversal notice that restructures the scene (the love named at 13:1 now inverted), opening a distinct expulsion action with its own protest, order, and execution; the two movements (force in, thrust out) are the narrative's designed symmetry and are separated by the reversal formula.

boundary_rationale: Absalom's reception speech 'Has Amnon your brother been with you? But now hold your peace, my sister' (web:2Sam.13.20) opens the aftermath: Tamar's desolate residence in Absalom's house (13:20b), King David's anger notice (web:2Sam.13.21), and the closing hatred summary 'Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad; for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had forced his sister Tamar' (web:2Sam.13.22) — a triple-household disposition (sister sheltered, father angry, brother silent) that seeds the revenge. Before the two-year gap the WLC opens a new parashah (petuchah after 13:22, single-witness; weak corroboration in the Prophets), reflecting the same pause the hatred-summary creates.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the aftermath to the expulsion scene — rejected because 13:20 changes location and participants (from Amnon's chamber to Absalom's house) via Tamar's exit-journey at 13:19, and the aftermath's texture is summary-notice (residence, anger, silence) rather than scene: the crying procession is the hinge, and the units divide where the narration's clock widens.

boundary_rationale: The time-gap formula 'After two full years' with the Baal Hazor sheep-shearing setting (web:2Sam.13.23) opens the invitation intrigue: Absalom's invitation to the king (13:24), the royal decline with blessing (web:2Sam.13.25), the pointed fallback request 'please let my brother Amnon go with us' met by the suspicious 'Why should he go with you?' (web:2Sam.13.26), and the pressed consent releasing Amnon and all the king's sons (web:2Sam.13.27) — the maneuvering complete when the victim is delivered. A closed spacing after 13:27 (single-witness) offers this seam its small assent.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running into the murder order 13:28-29 — rejected because 13:28 shifts scene and addressee to Absalom's servants at the feast with a command speech ('when Amnon's heart is merry with wine… Strike Amnon'): the court negotiation and the feast execution are separate stations, seamed at the changed audience.

boundary_rationale: The command formula 'Absalom commanded his servants, saying' (web:2Sam.13.28) opens the execution unit: the wine-merry timing signal, the strike order with its courage formula ('Don't be afraid… Be courageous, and be valiant'), and the compliance-plus-panic close 'The servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose, and every man got up on his mule and fled' (web:2Sam.13.29) — order, deed, and stampede in one tight action pair.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending to the false report 13:30 — rejected because 13:30 opens with a travel-synchronized report formula ('While they were on the way, the news came to David') relocating the narrative to Jerusalem and to a new information plot (the exaggerated all-sons-dead rumor); deed and rumor are distinct scenes joined only by the fleeing mules.

boundary_rationale: The synchronized report formula 'While they were on the way, the news came to David, saying, Absalom has slain all the king's sons' (web:2Sam.13.30) opens the rumor scene: the king's tearing and prostration with his servants' torn clothes (web:2Sam.13.31), and Jonadab's correcting speech -- only Amnon is dead, determined 'from the day that he forced his sister Tamar' (web:2Sam.13.32) -- with its reassurance close 'for only Amnon is dead' (web:2Sam.13.33). The scribal spacing here is busy — samekh intervals at 13:30 and 13:31, an open break at 13:33, all single-witness — but these can only murmur agreement; the drivers are the report formula and the completed correction.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending through the watchman verification 13:34-36 -- rejected because 13:34 pivots on a fresh observational frame, not on any change of speaker: the verse's watchman clause is hinneh-marked ('the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and, behold, many people were coming' -- oshb:2Sam.13.34 וַיִּשָּׂא הַנַּעַר הַצֹּפֶה...וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה עַם רַב הֹלְכִים), moving the narration from verbal correction to visual confirmation. The verse's own opening clause, וַיִּבְרַח אַבְשָׁלוֹם ('Absalom fled'), is a plain narrative wayyiqtol continuing the story's verb chain rather than a disjunctive; the genuinely fronted, disjunctive form of the same flight notice -- וְאַבְשָׁלוֹם בָּרַח -- belongs to 13:37 and 13:38, outside this span. Rumor-correction and arrival-verification remain two panels regardless: the watchman's new sight-line is itself sufficient to mark the seam.

boundary_rationale: The verification panel opens not on a disjunctive but on the watchman's fresh observational frame at 13:34: oshb:2Sam.13.34 reads וַיִּשָּׂא הַנַּעַר הַצֹּפֶה אֶת עינו עֵינָיו (ketiv/qere) וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה עַם רַב הֹלְכִים מִדֶּרֶךְ אַחֲרָיו מִצַּד הָהָר ('the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming...') -- a hinneh-marked sighting that turns the narration from Jonadab's spoken correction to visual confirmation. The verse's own opening clause, וַיִּבְרַח אַבְשָׁלוֹם ('Absalom fled'), is a plain narrative wayyiqtol continuing the story's verb chain, not a disjunctive; WEB's 'But' supplies an adversative sense the Hebrew syntax does not carry there. Jonadab's vindicated report follows at 13:35, הִנֵּה בְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ בָּאוּ כִּדְבַר עַבְדְּךָ כֵּן הָיָה ('Behold, the king's sons are coming! It is as your servant said'), and the arrival closes on communal weeping at 13:36 (וַיְהִי כְּכַלֹּתוֹ לְדַבֵּר וְהִנֵּה בְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ בָּאוּ...בָּכוּ בְּכִי גָּדוֹל מְאֹד), confirming the correction and closing the Jerusalem reception of the murder.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the Geshur flight notices 13:37-38 -- rejected because those two verses re-sound the flight report in a genuinely disjunctive register with a new destination and duration: both open וְאַבְשָׁלוֹם בָּרַח (waw + fronted subject + qatal -- 'And Absalom had fled...'), switching from scene time (the weeping arrival of 13:36) to summary time (years of exile). The flight notice thus occurs three times in the chapter (13:34, 37, 38), but only the latter two are syntactically disjunctive; 13:34's is a plain wayyiqtol embedded in a continuing narrative chain. The refrain observation survives this correction -- 13:34/37/38 remain a meaningful three-part echo -- but only 13:37-38 supply the syntactic marking the campaign elsewhere treats as tier-1 evidence.

boundary_rationale: The doubled flight-and-destination notices — 'Absalom fled and went to Talmai… king of Geshur. David mourned for his son every day' (web:2Sam.13.37) and the three-year duration (web:2Sam.13.38) — form an exile summary in durative register, closed by the longing notice 'King David longed to go out to Absalom, for he was comforted concerning Amnon' (web:2Sam.13.39), the psychological pivot on which Joab's ch 14 device turns. The codex rests after 13:39 with a setumah (single-witness) just where the exile summary hands off to Joab's perception — corroboration in the weak tier.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Placing 13:39 with ch 14's Joab unit as its motivation — rejected because 14:1 opens with Joab's perception formula ('Now Joab… perceived that the king's heart was toward Absalom') which presupposes and reports 13:39's state: the longing is the exile summary's close, the perception its uptake, and the participant change (David's interior to Joab's initiative) is the seam.

boundary_rationale: Joab's perception formula 'Now Joab the son of Zeruiah perceived that the king's heart was toward Absalom' (web:2Sam.14.1) opens the device unit: the fetch of the wise woman from Tekoa with the mourner-costume instructions (web:2Sam.14.2), the go-to-the-king commission, and the closing coaching notice 'So Joab put the words in her mouth' (web:2Sam.14.3) — preparation complete, script installed, before the performance begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running preparation into the audience 14:4 — rejected because 14:4 opens the performance with the woman's entrance formula ('When the woman of Tekoa spoke to the king, she fell on her face… Help, O king!'), a change of location (to the court) and of active speaker; the coaching notice at 14:3 is the preparation's formal close, exactly parallel to 13:5's script-then-enactment seam.

boundary_rationale: The performance opens with the petition formula 'Help, O king!' (web:2Sam.14.4) and runs the fictional case to its secured ruling: the widow's two-sons narrative with the family's demand and the quenched-coal figure (web:2Sam.14.5-7), the king's initial dismissal (14:8), the woman's guilt-transfer press (14:9), the stronger protection promise (14:10), and the climactic oath 'As Yahweh lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the earth' (web:2Sam.14.11) — the entrapment's trigger, secured before the application. Two spacing marks land inside this negotiation (an open break after 14:7, a closed one after 14:9, both single-witness); mid-scene layout cannot make edges, and the unit's true bounds are the petition formula and the sworn ruling.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at the king's first response 14:8 — rejected because the woman's follow-up presses the same case in the same audience until the oath of 14:11 secures an irrevocable ruling (the escalation from promise to oath is the case's designed arc); a split at any intermediate response would sever the negotiation the parable needs complete, the same logic that kept 12:1-6 whole.

boundary_rationale: The permission formula 'Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king' answered by 'Say on' (web:2Sam.14.12) pivots the audience from fictional case to application: the accusation-question 'Why then have you devised such a thing against the people of God?' with the banished-one charge (web:2Sam.14.13), the water-spilled-on-the-ground mortality theology with God's devising-means clause (web:2Sam.14.14), and the framed retreat into petition etiquette closing on the angel-of-God discernment blessing (web:2Sam.14.15-17). Both of this speech's edges happen to coincide with scribal intervals — samekh after 14:12, petuchah after 14:17, each single-witness — a pleasing symmetry that still ranks below the true driver: the marked permission-turn redirecting the speech to the king's own case, parallel to Nathan's 'You are the man' (12:7).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping case and application as one audience unit 14:4-17 — rejected because the permission exchange at 14:12 is an explicit discourse re-framing (the woman requests and receives leave for a different word), the same genre pivot that separates 12:1-6 from 12:7-12; without the split the parable's two-stage rhetoric (secure ruling, then apply it) is flattened.

boundary_rationale: The king's counter-interrogation formula 'Please don't hide anything from me that I ask you' (web:2Sam.14.18) reverses the audience's direction: the is-Joab's-hand-with-you question (web:2Sam.14.19), the woman's oath-framed confession 'your servant Joab urged me, and he put all these words in the mouth of your servant', and the closing angel-wisdom flattery 'My lord is wise… to know all things that are in the earth' (web:2Sam.14.20) — the device unmasked and the performance dissolved. One closed break after 14:20 (single-witness) trails the unmasking, worth noting and little else.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the unmasking to the application speech — rejected because 14:18 transfers the interrogative initiative from woman to king (he now asks, she answers), a marked role reversal within the audience that closes the scripted performance and opens its exposure; the confession formally returns authorship to Joab, whom the next unit addresses directly.

boundary_rationale: The address switch to Joab — 'The king said to Joab, Behold now, I have granted this thing. Go therefore, and bring the young man Absalom back' (web:2Sam.14.21) — opens the grant exchange: Joab's prostration, blessing, and favor-acknowledgment speech (web:2Sam.14.22) complete the two-turn transaction that authorizes the recall. The changed addressee (from the woman to Joab, now evidently present) is the boundary driver.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending into the journey 14:23-24 — rejected because 14:23 opens with Joab's rising-and-going itinerary ('So Joab arose and went to Geshur') executing the grant across a location change, while the grant unit is the court exchange itself; commission and execution divide at the movement formula, as at 9:4/9:5.

boundary_rationale: The itinerary formula 'So Joab arose and went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem' (web:2Sam.14.23) executes the recall, and the king's restriction 'Let him return to his own house, but let him not see my face' with its immediate enactment notice (web:2Sam.14.24) closes the unit on the half-pardon that governs the next two years. That the codex breaks around both verses (open after 14:23, closed after 14:24, single-witness apiece) is agreeable; the drivers remain the journey formula and the completed restriction.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the beauty parenthesis 14:25-27 — rejected because 14:25 opens a disjunctive narrator excursus ('Now in all Israel there was no one to be so much praised as Absalom') in descriptive register (beauty, hair-weight, children) wholly outside the recall's event line; the aside is its own register unit on the 4:4 parenthesis standard.

boundary_rationale: A disjunctive narrator excursus — 'Now in all Israel there was no one to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty. From the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no defect' (web:2Sam.14.25) — steps out of the event line into description: the annual hair-cutting with its two-hundred-shekel weight 'after the king's weight' (web:2Sam.14.26, including the WEB metrological footnote as translation metadata only), and the children notice naming the daughter Tamar 'a woman with a beautiful face' (web:2Sam.14.27), an echo-naming that ties the excursus to the violated aunt. The excursus ends where the manuscript also opens a new section — petuchah at 14:27, single-witness — layout seconding register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Distributing these notices into the surrounding narrative units — rejected because all three verses share one off-storyline descriptive register (no wayyiqtol event chain advances) and together build the physical-charisma dossier the revolt narrative presupposes; the campaign's aside standard (4:4; Ruth 2:1) keeps such excursuses as their own register units.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (two-year exclusion and the burnt field)
boundary_rationale: The duration notice resuming the restriction's key phrase -- 'Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, and he didn't see the king's face' (web:2Sam.14.28) -- re-enters the event line. The clause is a verbatim resumptive repetition (Wiederaufnahme) of 14:24's close, וּפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא רָאָה ('and did not see the king's face'), which is the final clause of the preceding unit (M8-2Sam-084) rather than this span's own edge; the repetition signals continuity across the intervening 14:25-27 beauty-and-household excursus rather than bracketing this span, since only one of the two matching phrases (14:28) lies inside 14:28-30. What follows is: the two refused summonses of Joab (web:2Sam.14.29), and the field-burning order with its execution 'So Absalom's servants set the field on fire' (web:2Sam.14.30) -- escalation complete, provocation delivered. Ahead of Joab's arrival the WLC turns a fresh parashah (petuchah after 14:30, single-witness); the arson, not the spacing, forces the scene change.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending to Joab's confrontation 14:31 -- rejected because 14:31 opens with Joab's rising-and-coming movement formula ('Then Joab arose and came to Absalom to his house') answering the provocation in person -- a participant-arrival seam; the exclusion unit closes on the arson that forces it.

boundary_rationale: Joab's arrival formula 'Then Joab arose and came to Absalom to his house' with the why-did-you-burn question (web:2Sam.14.31) opens the resolution: Absalom's quoted-within-quoted demand speech — 'let me see the king's face; and if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me' (web:2Sam.14.32) — and the brokered audience closing the chapter's arc in the wordless royal kiss 'and the king kissed Absalom' (web:2Sam.14.33), the face-seeing granted at last. The kiss that closes the arc is followed by the codex's own full stop, a petuchah at 14:33 (single-witness) — an echo, not an argument.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the audience 14:33 from the confrontation 14:31-32 — rejected because 14:33's audience is the immediate discharge of the demand Joab carries ('So Joab came to the king and told him; and when he had called for Absalom…') in one unbroken relay — provocation, demand, transmission, kiss — with no intervening scene; the kiss is the unit's designed closure, not a new episode.

boundary_rationale: The episode-opening formula 'After this' with the chariot-horses-and-fifty-runners acquisition (web:2Sam.15.1) launches the usurpation prologue: the early-rising gate routine with its scripted sympathy dialogue (web:2Sam.15.2-3), the oh-that-I-were-judge wish (web:2Sam.15.4), the handshake-and-kiss gesture protocol (15:5), and the iterative summary close 'So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel' (web:2Sam.15.6) — a habitual-action unit (iterative frames 'when any man…') whose theft metaphor seals it. The stolen-hearts summary is met in the manuscript by an open division after 15:6 (single-witness), scribal punctuation for a close the iterative frame already made.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the wish-speech 15:4 as its own unit — rejected because the whole passage is cast in iterative aspect ('It was so, that when any man came near…') describing a repeated routine, not single scenes: the speeches are the routine's script, and only the summary verse closes the pattern; no participant or scene boundary exists inside a habitual frame.

boundary_rationale: The time formula 'At the end of forty years' (web:2Sam.15.7) opens the pretext exchange: Absalom's Hebron vow-payment request with the quoted Geshur vow (web:2Sam.15.8), and the king's release 'Go in peace' with the departure itinerary 'So he arose and went to Hebron' (web:2Sam.15.9) -- request, grant, and movement completing the exchange that puts the pretender in the rival capital. As the narrative turns covert, the codex too starts fresh — petuchah after 15:9, single-witness — a parallel track to the seam the adversative dispatch creates.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending through the spy network 15:10-12 -- rejected because 15:10 opens a covert counter-action against the just-granted innocent pretext: 'Absalom sent spies throughout all the tribes' translates a plain narrative wayyiqtol dispatch formula, וַיִּשְׁלַח אַבְשָׁלוֹם מְרַגְּלִים בְּכָל שִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֵאמֹר (oshb:2Sam.15.10) -- not an adversative construction, since the Hebrew fronts no constituent before the verb. The seam is carried instead by the dispatch formula itself (וישלח + object + לאמר) together with the new addressees (כָּל שִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, 'all the tribes of Israel'), switching from court dialogue to conspiracy logistics; the irony still depends on this seam, since the vow-release and the covert dispatch stand in the same chapter without any narrator comment bridging them.

boundary_rationale: The covert dispatch 'But Absalom sent spies throughout all the tribes of Israel' with the trumpet-signal script 'Absalom is king in Hebron!' (web:2Sam.15.10) opens the conspiracy dossier: the two hundred unwitting invitees (web:2Sam.15.11), the summons of Ahithophel the Gilonite during the sacrifices, and the crescendo notice 'The conspiracy was strong, for the people increased continually with Absalom' (web:2Sam.15.12) — a summary close measuring the threat the next unit reports to David.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the messenger report 15:13 — rejected because 15:13 relocates to David's Jerusalem with an arrival formula ('A messenger came to David, saying') opening the flight narrative: the conspiracy dossier is Absalom-side material closed by its own strength-notice, and the report is the David-side uptake.

boundary_rationale: The messenger-arrival formula 'A messenger came to David, saying, The hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom' (web:2Sam.15.13 -- echoing 15:6's stolen hearts) triggers the flight: David's arise-and-flee speech with its sword-on-the-city fear (web:2Sam.15.14), the servants' readiness reply (15:15), the double going-out notices with the ten concubines left to keep the house (web:2Sam.15.16), the halt at Beth Merhak (web:2Sam.15.17), and the loyalist muster-roll -- Cherethites, Pelethites, and six hundred Gittites (web:2Sam.15.18, register-formula) -- which stages the Ittai exchange.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the muster-roll 15:16-18 from the decision 15:13-15 -- rejected because the going-out notices are the flee-command's immediate execution in one continuous evacuation movement (speech, assent, exit, halt, review), and the register verse is the review's content: the seam falls where the king singles out Ittai with a speech formula at 15:19, not inside the procession.

boundary_rationale: The address formula singling out one figure from the muster — 'Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, Why do you also go with us?' (web:2Sam.15.19) — opens the loyalty test: David's return-and-mercy release speech (15:19-20), Ittai's life-oath 'in what place my lord the king is, whether for death or for life, your servant will be there also' (web:2Sam.15.21), and the admission 'Go and pass over' with the passing of Ittai's whole company (web:2Sam.15.22) — test, oath, and acceptance complete.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the exchange into the evacuation procession — rejected because the exchange is a bounded two-party dialogue with its own test-and-oath arc inside the halt (the procession resumes only at 15:22's passing-over), and the campaign's audience-unit standard separates marked dialogue scenes from the itinerary that frames them.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (Kidron crossing and the ark returned)
boundary_rationale: The national-weeping crossing notice — 'All the country wept with a loud voice… The king also himself passed over the brook Kidron' (web:2Sam.15.23) — opens the ark panel: Zadok, the Levites, and the set-down ark with Abiathar (web:2Sam.15.24, hinneh-fronted arrival), David's carry-it-back speech with its submission theology 'if he says, I have no delight in you… let him do to me as seems good to him' (web:2Sam.15.25-26), the seer instructions establishing the two-sons intelligence channel and the fords rendezvous (web:2Sam.15.27-28), and the execution notice 'Zadok therefore and Abiathar carried God's ark to Jerusalem again' (web:2Sam.15.29) — command and compliance closing the panel. The samekh interval the codex places after 15:26 (single-witness) sits inside David's continuing address to Zadok; spacing inside a speech divides nothing.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the intelligence instructions 15:27-28 from the ark-return speech — rejected because both speeches are delivered to Zadok in one roadside audience ('The king said also to Zadok' is a turn-marker continuing the same address), and 15:29's single execution notice discharges both; the panel's unity is the ark-and-priests disposition.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (Olivet ascent and the Ahithophel prayer)
boundary_rationale: The ascent tableau — 'David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, and wept as he went up… head covered and went barefoot' with the people's mirrored mourning (web:2Sam.15.30) — carries the procession onto the mount, where the conspiracy report 'Ahithophel is among the conspirators' triggers David's counter-prayer 'Yahweh, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness' (web:2Sam.15.31) — the petition whose answer arrives in the very next unit; tableau and prayer form the ascent's paired panel.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the prayer to the Hushai commission 15:32-37 — rejected because 15:32 opens with an arrival-at-place formula ('When David had come to the top, where God was worshiped, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him') that marks a station change (mid-ascent to summit) and a new participant: the narrative deliberately seams prayer from answer so that Hushai's appearance reads as providence.

boundary_rationale: The summit-arrival formula with hinneh-marked meeting — 'When David had come to the top, where God was worshiped, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his tunic torn' (web:2Sam.15.32) — opens the commissioning: the burden-versus-agent alternative (15:33), the scripted defection speech to plant in Absalom's court (web:2Sam.15.34), the priests-and-sons relay protocol (web:2Sam.15.35-36), and the double entry close 'So Hushai, David's friend, came into the city; and Absalom came into Jerusalem' (web:2Sam.15.37) — a synchronized two-party arrival that ends the flight sequence and stages the counsel duel.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the double-entry notice 15:37 as a frame verse — rejected because the notice is the commission's execution (Hushai goes as instructed) fused with Absalom's arrival in one sentence-pair: the synchrony is the unit's designed close, planting agent and target together, and no formula separates it from the commission it discharges.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (Ziba's provisions and the slander grant)
boundary_rationale: The itinerary-station formula 'When David was a little past the top, behold, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him' with the provision inventory (web:2Sam.16.1, register-formula: donkeys, loaves, raisins, summer fruits, wine) opens the encounter: the what-do-you-mean question and Ziba's itemized answer (web:2Sam.16.2), the where-is-your-master's-son question with the slander reply quoting Mephibosheth's alleged restoration hope (web:2Sam.16.3), and the summary transfer 'all that belongs to Mephibosheth is yours' with Ziba's obeisance (web:2Sam.16.4) — grant given, encounter closed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging with the Shimei encounter — rejected because 16:5 opens a new station with its own arrival formula ('When King David came to Bahurim, behold, a man… came out') and an opposite dramatic charge (gift versus curse): the flight's road-encounters are a paired sequence whose stations the itinerary formulas separate.

boundary_rationale: The Bahurim arrival formula with hinneh-marked emergence — 'When King David came to Bahurim, behold, a man of the family of Saul's house came out… and cursed as he came' (web:2Sam.16.5) — opens one continuous roadside scene: the stone-throwing (16:6), Shimei's man-of-blood curse speech (web:2Sam.16.7-8), Abishai's dead-dog offer and David's sons-of-Zeruiah rebuke (web:2Sam.16.9-10), the let-him-curse theology with its repayment hope (web:2Sam.16.11-12), the parallel-march notice with Shimei cursing along the hillside (16:13), and the weary-arrival refreshment close (web:2Sam.16.14) that ends the whole flight itinerary. Abishai's intervention is a turn within the scene (he is already in the column), not a scene change; the cluster of spacing marks the codex scatters through the encounter (16:9, 16:10, 16:13, single-witness) likewise divides speech-turns, not scenes.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the curse 16:5-8 from David's response 16:9-14 — rejected because the response turns happen at the same station with the same participant-set (Shimei still cursing through 16:13, the column still marching): the named-speaker formulas at 16:9/16:10/16:11 are turn-markers inside one gauntlet scene, and the campaign's turn-marker principle keeps the encounter whole through its itinerary close.

boundary_rationale: The counter-arrival notice 'Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him' (web:2Sam.16.15) switches the narrative to the usurper's court: Hushai's double-shouted 'Long live the king!' (web:2Sam.16.16), Absalom's is-this-your-kindness challenge (web:2Sam.16.17), and Hushai's studied ambiguity — 'whomever Yahweh and this people… have chosen, I will be his' with the serve-in-the-son's-presence equivocation (web:2Sam.16.18-19) — the infiltration accomplished when the homage is accepted. The audience's dismissal coincides with an open parashah after 16:19 in the single WLC witness — corroborative color for a boundary the address-switch draws.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the counsel scene 16:20-23 — rejected because 16:20 opens a new deliberative session with a fresh address formula ('Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, Give your counsel') and a different adviser on the floor: the homage audience (testing Hushai) and the counsel session (consulting Ahithophel) are distinct court proceedings.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (Ahithophel's first counsel and the rooftop tent)
boundary_rationale: The counsel-request formula 'Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, Give your counsel what we shall do' (web:2Sam.16.20) opens the session: the concubine counsel with its strengthen-the-hands rationale (web:2Sam.16.21), the rooftop-tent execution 'in the sight of all Israel' (web:2Sam.16.22 — enacting 12:11-12's before-the-sun sentence), and the narrator's evaluative close on Ahithophel's counsel 'as if a man inquired at the inner sanctuary of God' (web:2Sam.16.23) — an oracle-simile aside that calibrates the stakes of the coming counsel duel. The oracle-simile aside is trailed by a setumah at 16:23 (single-witness), the scribal layout resting where the session ends.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching the evaluation 16:23 as a standalone narrator aside — rejected because the verse's function is bound to this session (it explains why 16:21's counsel was followed without question and why defeating such counsel in ch 17 requires divine intervention): it is the session's closing frame rather than a free-floating excursus, parallel to the in-scene evaluative closes at 3:36-37.

boundary_rationale: A fresh counsel speech — 'Moreover Ahithophel said to Absalom, Let me now choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue after David tonight' (web:2Sam.17.1) — opens the second session of the counsel duel: the strike-the-king-only surgical plan with its bring-back-the-people close (web:2Sam.17.2-3), and the approval notice 'The saying pleased Absalom well, and all the elders of Israel' (web:2Sam.17.4) — counsel given and provisionally accepted, before Hushai is called. A closed interval after 17:4 (single-witness; in the Prophets these count for little) matches the approval-notice close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching this counsel to 16:20-23 as one Ahithophel session — rejected because 16:23's narrator evaluation formally closed the first session (its oracle-simile is a session-frame), and 17:1's proposal opens a new deliberative item (military pursuit versus the concubine legitimation) that receives its own separate approval notice; the counsel duel's structure needs the two counsels of Ahithophel distinct.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (Hushai's counter-counsel and the ordained verdict)
boundary_rationale: The summons 'Now call Hushai the Archite also, and let's hear likewise what he says' (web:2Sam.17.5) opens the counter-counsel movement: the consultation question (17:6), Hushai's not-good verdict (web:2Sam.17.7), the bear-robbed-of-cubs and pit-hidden fear rhetoric (web:2Sam.17.8-10), the sand-by-the-sea muster counsel with the dew-fall and ropes-to-the-river hyperboles (web:2Sam.17.11-13), and the double close -- the court's verdict 'The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better' and the narrator's theological key 'For Yahweh had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that Yahweh might bring evil on Absalom' (web:2Sam.17.14) -- the answer to 15:31's prayer, sealing the duel. The ordination verdict is followed by the codex's samekh space at 17:14 (single-witness), a grace note under the theological key.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the verdict-and-ordination verse 17:14 as a narrator unit -- rejected because the verdict clause is the assembly's own speech act completing the session (proposal, counter-proposal, decision), and the ordination clause is its inseparable narratorial explanation. The two clauses are paratactic rather than subordinate in the Hebrew: 17:14's second half opens וַיהוָה צִוָּה לְהָפֵר אֶת עֲצַת אֲחִיתֹפֶל הַטּוֹבָה ('and Yahweh had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel') with waw + fronted subject יהוה + qatal -- a coordinate disjunctive clause carrying no כי or אשר, so 'for' is the WEB's connective rather than a Hebrew subordinator. The fronted subject is itself what marks the clause as the narrator's evaluative counterpart to the assembly's verdict in the same verse, which supports keeping the verse whole at least as well as a claimed logical dependency would: severing the session from its outcome would still leave the duel undecided, as with the verdict closes at 3:36-39.

boundary_rationale: The address switch out of Absalom's court -- 'Then Hushai said to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests' (web:2Sam.17.15) -- opens the dispatch: the two-counsels report and the urgent relay instruction. MT 17:16 reads אַל תָּלֶן הַלַּיְלָה בְּעַרְבוֹת הַמִּדְבָּר, 'Don't lodge tonight in the plains of the wilderness' (עַרְבוֹת, with no ketiv/qere variant at this verse), followed by the emphatic infinitive-absolute crossing command וְגַם עָבוֹר תַּעֲבוֹר, 'but by all means pass over' -- message composed and handed to the channel established at 15:35-36, activating the relay the next unit runs. (WEB's 'fords' at 17:16 harmonizes to 15:28's genuine ketiv/qere pair, בעברות/בְּעַרְבוֹת, which is the only verse in the book carrying that variant; 17:16 itself has no textual warrant for 'fords'.)
strongest_rejected_alternative: Fusing the dispatch with the relay adventure 17:17-21 -- rejected because 17:17 opens with a disjunctive setting frame on new participants ('Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying by En Rogel; and a female servant used to go and report') shifting from Hushai's instruction to the couriers' station and their peril-episode; sender and channel are distinct narrative stations.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (courier relay, the well at Bahurim, and the night crossing)
boundary_rationale: The disjunctive courier frame 'Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying by En Rogel' with the maidservant relay protocol (web:2Sam.17.17) opens the transmission adventure: the boy's sighting and the flight to the Bahurim well (web:2Sam.17.18), the covering-and-grain ruse (17:19), the searchers' misdirected question-and-return (web:2Sam.17.20), the emergence and delivery 'Arise and pass quickly over the water; for thus has Ahithophel counseled against you' (web:2Sam.17.21), and the command's execution — David's night crossing complete by morning light with not one lacking (web:2Sam.17.22) — message discharged in movement, on the command-execution pattern of 5:25. One spacing mark interrupts the episode's middle (setumah after 17:20, single-witness); an adventure in continuous motion cannot be cut by layout.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching the crossing 17:22 as its own itinerary unit — rejected because 17:22's wayyiqtol chain is the immediate uptake of 17:21's imperative within one night's continuous action (warn, rise, cross by morning): the relay's purpose clause is only closed by the completed crossing, and no formula intervenes.

boundary_rationale: A self-contained single-verse obituary — 'When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey, arose, and went home to his city, set his house in order, and hanged himself; and he died, and was buried in the tomb of his father' (web:2Sam.17.23) — a complete micro-narrative (perception, journey, testament, death, burial) in one verse, detached from both the crossing before it and the war positioning after it, on the single-verse notice standard of 3:1 and 11:1. Its isolation is mirrored by the setumah the codex sets after 17:23 (single-witness) — the obituary boxed off by scribes as by syntax.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the suicide to the counsel-duel unit as Ahithophel's exit — rejected because the intervening relay-and-crossing episode (17:17-22) has already moved the narrative clock and location: the notice is a deliberately displaced epilogue whose perception clause ('saw that his counsel was not followed') retrospects the duel across the seam, functioning as a freestanding closure notice for the counselor's whole arc.

boundary_rationale: The double arrival notice 'Then David came to Mahanaim. Absalom passed over the Jordan' (web:2Sam.17.24) opens the pre-battle positioning: Amasa's appointment over the army in Joab's place with the narrator's genealogical parenthesis linking him to Zeruiah's sister (web:2Sam.17.25), and the encampment notice 'Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead' (web:2Sam.17.26) — both sides placed on the board. Before the provisioning register the manuscript inserts one more samekh pause (after 17:26, single-witness), congruent with the positioning panel's end.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the provisioning 17:27-29 — rejected because 17:27 re-opens with its own arrival-station formula ('When David had come to Mahanaim') introducing a three-benefactor list and a goods register — a register-formula unit distinct from the troop-positioning notices; the repeated Mahanaim arrival is the formal re-entry marking the new unit.

boundary_rationale: The station formula 'When David had come to Mahanaim' (web:2Sam.17.27) heads a formal register: three named benefactors with full patronymics and towns — Shobi of Rabbah, Machir of Lo Debar (the same householder of 9:4), Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim — and the itemized goods catalogue of beds, vessels, and eleven foodstuffs (web:2Sam.17.28-29a), closed by the rationale quotation 'The people are hungry, weary, and thirsty in the wilderness' (web:2Sam.17.29). Per the list-register rule the catalogue is one cumulative unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the goods catalogue from the benefactor names — rejected because the register is one syntactic span (the three subjects of 17:27 govern the verb 'brought' whose objects run through 17:29): names and goods form a single list-sentence that cannot be severed without breaking the clause.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (muster, gate review, and the deal-gently command)
boundary_rationale: The muster formula 'David counted the people who were with him, and set captains' (web:2Sam.18.1) opens the pre-battle scene: the three-thirds division under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai with the king's I-will-go declaration (web:2Sam.18.2), the people's you-are-worth-ten-thousand refusal (web:2Sam.18.3), the concession and gate review (18:4), and the public charge 'Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom' heard by all the people (web:2Sam.18.5) — the command whose public audibility the oak scene will invoke (18:12). Two closed intervals land inside this one gate-review scene (after 18:2 and 18:3, single-witness); dialogue turns attract spacing, but spacing does not make seams.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the deal-gently command 18:5 as its own unit — rejected because the command is issued at the same gate review to the just-named captains as the marching columns pass (one scene, one occasion), and its narrative weight depends on the whole army's presence established by the review; the seam falls at 18:6's movement into the field.

boundary_rationale: The deployment formula 'So the people went out into the field against Israel; and the battle was in the forest of Ephraim' (web:2Sam.18.6) opens a compressed battle summary: the twenty-thousand slaughter notice (web:2Sam.18.7) and the summarizing paradox 'the forest devoured more people that day than the sword devoured' (web:2Sam.18.8) — a narrator's battle-verdict in summary register, closed before the lens narrows to one rider.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending into the oak episode 18:9 — rejected because 18:9 shifts from summary register to scene register with a chance-encounter formula ('Absalom happened to meet David's servants') and a single named participant: the wide-shot battle and the close-shot Absalom scene are different narrative registers the text separates cleanly.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (Absalom in the oak and Joab's kill)
boundary_rationale: The chance-encounter formula 'Absalom happened to meet David's servants' with the mule-and-oak suspension tableau — 'hanging between the sky and earth' (web:2Sam.18.9) — opens the death scene: the anonymous man's report to Joab (18:10), Joab's why-didn't-you-strike rebuke with its ten-silver offer (web:2Sam.18.11), the man's refusal citing the publicly heard royal command 'Beware that no one touch the young man Absalom' (web:2Sam.18.12-13), Joab's impatient 'I'm not going to wait like this with you' with the three darts through the heart (web:2Sam.18.14), and the armor-bearers' finishing blow (web:2Sam.18.15) — one continuous scene from suspension to death.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the Joab-informant debate 18:10-13 from the killing 18:14-15 — rejected because the debate and the deed occur in one unbroken exchange at one location (Joab breaks off the dialogue mid-scene — 'I'm not going to wait like this with you' — and acts): the refusal speech is the deed's foil, and no scene or participant boundary intervenes between rebuke and darts.

boundary_rationale: The trumpet-restraint formula 'Joab blew the trumpet, and the people returned from pursuing after Israel' (web:2Sam.18.16, the same signal-instrument close as 2:28) opens the battle's termination: the pit burial under 'a very great heap of stones' and the dispersal notice 'Then all Israel fled, each to his own tent' (web:2Sam.18.17) — cairn and flight closing the civil war's fighting. The cairn-and-flight close is echoed by a setumah at 18:17 (single-witness) before the monument parenthesis begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Including the monument aside 18:18 — rejected because 18:18 is a disjunctive narrator excursus ('Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself the pillar…') in retrospective register with a to-this-day formula: the ironic contrast between cairn and monument works precisely because the aside stands apart from the event line, per the 4:4/14:25-27 aside standard.

boundary_rationale: A single-verse disjunctive narrator parenthesis — 'Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself the pillar which is in the king's valley' with his quoted no-son rationale and the etiological close 'It is called Absalom's monument, to this day' (web:2Sam.18.18) — a retrospective excursus with to-this-day formula, standing outside the battle's event line as the ironic counter-image to the stone heap of 18:17, on the single-verse aside standard (4:4). A matching samekh space after 18:18 (single-witness) frames the aside on its far side as well.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the aside into the burial notice — rejected because the aside's tense and register (pluperfect retrospect, quoted motive, naming etiology) are wholly outside the battle-day timeline, and its no-son claim even stands in canonical tension with 14:27's three sons — a tension the map preserves by keeping the excursus distinct rather than harmonizing it into the narrative unit.

boundary_rationale: Ahimaaz's request formula 'Let me now run and carry the king news' (web:2Sam.18.19) opens the dispatch debate at the battlefield command post: Joab's refusal 'because the king's son is dead' (web:2Sam.18.20), the Cushite's commissioning and run (web:2Sam.18.21), Ahimaaz's twice-pressed come-what-may insistence -- 'come what may' appears once in his first plea (web:2Sam.18.22) and again in his second (web:2Sam.18.23) -- and the release 'Run!' with the overtaking notice 'Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the Plain, and outran the Cushite' (web:2Sam.18.23) -- both runners launched, the two-messenger suspense machine armed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the unit into the watchman scene 18:24 -- rejected because 18:24 relocates to Mahanaim with a disjunctive setting frame ('Now David was sitting between the two gates; and the watchman went up to the roof') switching viewpoint from senders to receiver: dispatch and reception are the relay's two stations, seamed at the location change.

boundary_rationale: The disjunctive setting frame 'Now David was sitting between the two gates; and the watchman went up to the roof… and, behold, a man running alone' (web:2Sam.18.24) opens the sighting scene: the alone-means-news inference (web:2Sam.18.25), the second runner's sighting (18:26), and the gait-recognition 'the running of the first one is like the running of Ahimaaz' with David's hopeful 'He is a good man, and comes with good news' (web:2Sam.18.27) — anticipation built to its peak before any word arrives.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Fusing the sighting with Ahimaaz's report 18:28-30 — rejected because 18:28 shifts from watching to hearing with the runner's arrival-and-call formula ('Ahimaaz called, and said to the king, All is well'), beginning the audience proper: the watchman panel (sight) and the report panels (speech) are the suspense structure's distinct stages.

boundary_rationale: The arrival-and-call formula 'Ahimaaz called, and said to the king, All is well' with the prostration and blessing (web:2Sam.18.28) opens the first report audience: the king's single question 'Is it well with the young man Absalom?' (web:2Sam.18.29), Ahimaaz's tumult evasion, and the stand-aside dismissal 'Come and stand here. He came and stood still' (web:2Sam.18.30) — the audience suspended unresolved, clearing the floor for the second runner. The setumah after 18:28 (single-witness) interrupts the first runner's audience mid-stream — layout again lagging behind the scene's own architecture.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Joining both reports 18:28-32 as one reception scene — rejected because the Cushite's arrival at 18:31 opens with its own hinneh-marked entrance formula ('Behold, the Cushite came') and repeats the question-answer pattern with the opposite outcome: the two-runner design pays off in two formally parallel but separate audiences, and the stand-aside notice closes the first.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (the Cushite's report and David's lament for Absalom)
boundary_rationale: The hinneh-marked entrance 'Behold, the Cushite came' with his good-news formula (web:2Sam.18.31) opens the second audience: the repeated Absalom question (web:2Sam.18.32), the Cushite's may-your-enemies-be-as-that-young-man disclosure, and the collapse -- David's ascent to the gate chamber weeping the fivefold 'My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! I wish I had died instead of you' (web:2Sam.18.33 = oshb:2Sam.19.1 (MT); all MT citations in this row are offset +1 per crosswalk within the WEB 18:33-19:43 = MT 19:1-19:44 segment) -- the lament that closes the battle-day narrative and hangs over the next scene. The 'fivefold' count is exact in the Hebrew: MT 19:1 reads בְּנִי אַבְשָׁלוֹם בְּנִי בְנִי אַבְשָׁלוֹם מִי יִתֵּן מוּתִי אֲנִי תַחְתֶּיךָ אַבְשָׁלוֹם בְּנִי בְנִי -- בני five times, אבשלום three. Though the codex spaces twice inside this exchange (after 18:31 and 18:32, single-witness), neither interval can outrank the entrance formula and the completed lament that actually bound the unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching the lament verse as the opening of the ch 19 mourning-crisis unit (as MT's chapter division does at MT 19:1) -- rejected because the lament is the audience's immediate outcome (question, answer, collapse in one unbroken sequence at the gate), while the report frame 'Joab was told, Behold, the king weeps' opens the next unit at WEB 19:1 = MT 19:2 (וַיֻּגַּד לְיוֹאָב הִנֵּה הַמֶּלֶךְ בֹּכֶה וַיִּתְאַבֵּל עַל אַבְשָׁלֹם), which presupposes the lament as accomplished fact. MT 19:1 itself is the lament verse (בְּנִי אַבְשָׁלוֹם בְּנִי בְנִי אַבְשָׁלוֹם...), not the report -- the report is one verse later, at MT 19:2. The WEB/MT chapter seam is metadata only and cannot outrank the scene's own causal chain.

boundary_rationale: The report frame 'Joab was told, Behold, the king weeps and mourns for Absalom' (web:2Sam.19.1 = oshb:2Sam.19.2 (MT); all ch-19 MT citations offset +1 per crosswalk) opens the crisis panel: the narrator's verdict 'The victory that day was turned into mourning' (web:2Sam.19.2), the army sneaking into the city 'as people who are ashamed steal away' (web:2Sam.19.3), and the king's covered face with the renewed cry 'My son Absalom, Absalom, my son, my son!' (web:2Sam.19.4 = oshb:2Sam.19.5 (MT)) — the lament refrain resounding as public fact, the state of affairs Joab's rebuke must break.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the panel to the 18:31-33 lament — rejected because 19:1 changes viewpoint and register: the lament scene is David's private collapse, while 19:1-4 is the public-consequence panel opened by a report-to-Joab frame and narrated as the whole army's day; the report formula is the seam.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (Joab's rebuke and the king restored to the gate)
boundary_rationale: Joab's entrance formula 'Joab came into the house to the king, and said' together with the you-have-shamed-your-servants indictment (web:2Sam.19.5 = oshb:2Sam.19.6 (MT), הֹבַשְׁתָּ הַיּוֹם אֶת פְּנֵי כָל עֲבָדֶיךָ) opens the confrontation. The love-haters antithesis follows one verse later, at web:2Sam.19.6 = oshb:2Sam.19.7 (MT), a genuine chiasm in the Hebrew, לְאַהֲבָה אֶת שֹׂנְאֶיךָ וְלִשְׂנֹא אֶת אֹהֲבֶיךָ ('to love your enemies and hate your friends'). The sworn ultimatum follows at web:2Sam.19.7 = oshb:2Sam.19.8 (MT), 'if you don't go out, not a man will stay with you this night,' carried by a real oath formula with the negative-oath particle אם (כִּי בַיהוָה נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי כִּי אֵינְךָ יוֹצֵא אִם יָלִין אִישׁ אִתְּךָ הַלַּיְלָה). The compliance close -- the king rises and sits in the gate with the people's return before him (web:2Sam.19.8 = oshb:2Sam.19.9 (MT)) -- command discharged in movement per the command-execution pattern, with the closing disjunctive 'Now Israel had fled every man to his tent' (וְיִשְׂרָאֵל נָס אִישׁ לְאֹהָלָיו, a genuine waw + fronted-subject + qatal construction) pivoting to the national question. In the Leningrad layout a samekh follows MT 19:9 (= WEB 19:8; single-witness), lightly seconding the compliance close. (All MT citations in this row are offset +1 per crosswalk within the WEB 18:33-19:43 = MT 19:1-19:44 segment.)
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching the compliance verse WEB 19:8 (= MT 19:9) to head the strife unit -- rejected because its rising-and-sitting is the direct discharge of WEB 19:7's (= MT 19:8) arise-and-go-out ultimatum within the same scene sequence (rebuke to compliance), while the strife deliberation opens with its own mass-subject frame at WEB 19:9 = MT 19:10, 'All the people were at strife throughout all the tribes' (וַיְהִי כָל הָעָם נָדוֹן בְּכָל שִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל) -- one verse later than the compliance close, not the same verse. Only the verse-final disjunctive of WEB 19:8/MT 19:9 (וְיִשְׂרָאֵל נָס אִישׁ לְאֹהָלָיו) belongs thematically ahead, and that hinge is disclosed here.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (tribal deliberation on the king's return)
boundary_rationale: The mass-deliberation frame 'All the people were at strife throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying' (web:2Sam.19.9 = oshb:2Sam.19.10 (MT)) opens a compact national-debate unit: the delivered-us recital, the fled-from-Absalom embarrassment, and the closing self-challenge 'why don't you speak a word of bringing the king back?' (web:2Sam.19.10) -- the popular groundswell to which David's Judah overture responds. The deliberation's end coincides with the codex's closed break at MT 19:11 (= WEB 19:10; single-witness) — coincidence with, not cause of, the seam. (All MT citations in this row are offset +1 per crosswalk within the WEB 18:33-19:43 = MT 19:1-19:44 segment.)
strongest_rejected_alternative: Fusing the deliberation with David's overture WEB 19:11-14 -- rejected because the royal messenger formula opens the new unit at WEB 19:11 = MT 19:12 (וְהַמֶּלֶךְ דָּוִד שָׁלַח אֶל צָדוֹק וְאֶל אֶבְיָתָר הַכֹּהֲנִים, 'King David sent to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests, saying, Speak to the elders of Judah') -- one verse after this span's own close at WEB 19:10 = MT 19:11 (the setumah verse). The initiative changes actors (tribes' talk to king's diplomacy) and audience (Israel's tribes to Judah's elders), a tier-1 dispatch seam.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (the Judah overture and Amasa oath)
boundary_rationale: The messenger formula 'King David sent to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests' (web:2Sam.19.11 = oshb:2Sam.19.12 (MT)) opens the diplomatic unit: the why-are-you-last challenge with the bone-and-flesh kinship appeal (web:2Sam.19.12), the sworn Amasa appointment 'God do so to me… if you aren't captain of the army before me continually instead of Joab' (web:2Sam.19.13), and the success notice 'He bowed the heart of all the men of Judah, even as one man' with their Return message (web:2Sam.19.14) — overture sent, oath given, hearts won.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending into the Jordan convoy 19:15 — rejected because 19:15 opens the physical return with a movement formula ('So the king returned, and came to the Jordan. Judah came to Gilgal') shifting from message diplomacy to itinerary: the overture unit closes on the campaign's success notice, and the journey is its own staged sequence.

boundary_rationale: The return-movement formula 'So the king returned, and came to the Jordan. Judah came to Gilgal, to go to meet the king' (web:2Sam.19.15 = oshb:2Sam.19.16 (MT)) opens the convoy panel: Shimei's hurried descent with the men of Judah (web:2Sam.19.16), and the muster of his thousand Benjamites with Ziba and his fifteen sons and twenty servants rushing to the Jordan (web:2Sam.19.17) — the reception apparatus assembled on the bank before the crossing audiences begin.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the panel through the ferry and prostration 19:18 — rejected because 19:18's second half opens the first pardon audience with Shimei's prostration formula ('Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king'), and verse-granular tiling assigns the hinge verse to the audience it initiates; the convoy panel is the wide-shot muster, the prostration the close-shot scene.

boundary_rationale: The ferry notice and prostration formula -- 'Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king when he had come over the Jordan' (web:2Sam.19.18 = oshb:2Sam.19.19 (MT)) -- open the pardon audience: Shimei's don't-impute-iniquity plea with his first-of-Joseph claim (web:2Sam.19.19-20), Abishai's shouldn't-he-die objection invoking the cursed anointed -- מְשִׁיחַ יְהוָה, the same phrase as 1:14/1:16 -- (web:2Sam.19.21), David's sons-of-Zeruiah rebuke with the shall-any-die-today kingship declaration, itself an almost verbatim repetition of the rebuke at 16:10 (web:2Sam.19.22), and the sworn pardon 'You will not die. The king swore to him' (web:2Sam.19.23 = oshb:2Sam.19.24 (MT)) -- plea, objection, and oath completing the audience, the mirror-scene of 16:5-14. The scribes space this pardon scene at its speech-turns (samekh intervals at MT 19:21, 19:22, 19:24 — WEB 19:20/21/23; single-witness), tracking the dialogue's rhythm rather than its boundaries. (All MT citations in this row are offset +1 per crosswalk within the WEB 18:33-19:43 = MT 19:1-19:44 segment.)
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Abishai's objection and David's rebuke (WEB 19:21-23 = MT 19:22-24) from the plea -- rejected because objection and pardon happen in the same riverside audience with the same participants standing before the king (Abishai's turn is an intervention inside the hearing, exactly as at 16:9): the audience's designed arc runs plea-objection-ruling, and the oath is its terminus.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (Mephibosheth's defense and the divided land)
boundary_rationale: A new claimant's arrival formula with a mourning-neglect description -- 'Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king; and he had neither groomed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes' (web:2Sam.19.24 = oshb:2Sam.19.25 (MT)) -- opens the second audience: the why-didn't-you-go question (web:2Sam.19.25 = oshb:2Sam.19.26 (MT)), the my-servant-deceived-me defense with the lameness claim and angel-of-God deference (web:2Sam.19.26-27 = oshb:2Sam.19.27-28 (MT)), the dead-men-at-your-table waiver of right (web:2Sam.19.28 = oshb:2Sam.19.29 (MT)), the impatient ruling 'you and Ziba divide the land' (web:2Sam.19.29 = oshb:2Sam.19.30 (MT)), and Mephibosheth's let-him-take-all close (web:2Sam.19.30 = oshb:2Sam.19.31 (MT)) -- an audience complete from arrival to renunciation, counter-weighing Ziba's 16:1-4 slander without the narrator adjudicating. The far edge is independently grounded by a tier-1 signal at the immediately following verse: oshb:2Sam.19.32 (MT; = WEB 19:31) opens וּבַרְזִלַּי הַגִּלְעָדִי יָרַד מֵרֹגְלִים, a waw + fronted-subject + qatal participant introduction marking the start of the next unit (Barzillai's episode) right after this span's close. Of the two scribal breaks in range only the closed one after MT 19:31 (= WEB 19:30, single-witness) abuts an edge of this audience; the open break after MT 19:29 (= WEB 19:28) interrupts Mephibosheth's waiver speech at the fifth of the span's seven verses, and an intra-speech interval decides nothing, exactly as sibling rows treat mid-scene marks. (All MT citations in this row are offset +1 per crosswalk within the WEB 18:33-19:43 = MT 19:1-19:44 segment.)
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the ruling (WEB 19:29-30 = MT 19:30-31) from the defense -- rejected because the ruling is the audience's own resolution turn (same participants, same station), and the renunciation reply is Mephibosheth's closing word in the exchange; severing verdict from hearing would leave both fragments incomplete, per the judicial-arc standard of 1:13-16 and 4:9-12.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (Barzillai's farewell and the Chimham substitution)
boundary_rationale: The third arrival formula — 'Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim' with the narrator's aged-benefactor recap of the Mahanaim provisioning (web:2Sam.19.31-32, tying back to 17:27-29) — opens the farewell audience: the come-over-with-me invitation (web:2Sam.19.33), Barzillai's eighty-years speech with its can-I-taste, can-I-hear renunciation and the die-by-my-parents'-grave petition substituting Chimham (web:2Sam.19.34-37), the king's grant 'Chimham shall go over with me… Whatever you request of me, that I will do for you' (web:2Sam.19.38), and the crossing close with the kiss, blessing, and return home (web:2Sam.19.39 = oshb:2Sam.19.40 (MT)) — the third and warmest of the three Jordan audiences, closed by the completed crossing. Samekh spacing appears at MT 19:38 and 19:40 (= WEB 19:37/19:39; single-witness), running alongside the farewell's grant and crossing without steering either.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Barzillai's speech 19:34-37 from its frame — rejected because invitation, refusal-speech, grant, and farewell kiss form one continuous two-party audience at one station (the riverbank), with each turn syntactically answering the last; the audience's own closure is the crossing-and-return notice, not any internal turn.

boundary_rationale: The Gilgal itinerary notice with the asymmetric escort — 'All the people of Judah brought the king over, and also half the people of Israel' (web:2Sam.19.40 = oshb:2Sam.19.41 (MT)) — opens the quarrel: Israel's stolen-you-away complaint (web:2Sam.19.41), Judah's close-relative defense with its have-we-eaten-at-the-king's-cost protest (web:2Sam.19.42), Israel's ten-parts counter-claim (web:2Sam.19.43), and the narrator's ominous close 'The words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel' (web:2Sam.19.43 = oshb:2Sam.19.44 (MT)) — the tinder the Sheba spark ignites. Here again the codex spaces the quarrel's turns (MT 19:42, 19:43, 19:44 = WEB 19:41/42/43; single-witness) — turn-tracking, while the escort notice and the fierceness verdict supply the edges.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the quarrel to 20:1's secession — rejected because 20:1 introduces a new named agent with a chance-presence formula ('There happened to be there a wicked fellow, whose name was Sheba') and a trumpet-signaled secession cry: the quarrel is mass dialogue between tribal blocs, the secession a single demagogue's act; the causal chain crosses the seam, but the formula marks the new unit.

boundary_rationale: The chance-presence formula introducing a named agitator — 'There happened to be there a wicked fellow, whose name was Sheba the son of Bichri, a Benjamite; and he blew the trumpet' (web:2Sam.20.1) — opens the secession unit: the no-portion-in-David cry 'Every man to his tents, Israel!' (a war-cry formula) and the split notice 'So all the men of Israel went up from following David, and followed Sheba… but the men of Judah joined with their king, from the Jordan even to Jerusalem' (web:2Sam.20.2) — call and cleavage complete in two verses.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending to the concubine notice 20:3 — rejected because 20:3 changes subject, location, and register entirely (David's Jerusalem homecoming and a durative household disposition running 'to the day of their death'), a closure notice for the 15:16 thread with no connection to the secession's event line.

boundary_rationale: A single-verse closure notice — 'David came to his house at Jerusalem; and the king took the ten women his concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in custody… So they were shut up to the day of their death, living in widowhood' (web:2Sam.20.3) — that resolves the thread planted at 15:16 and defiled at 16:21-22 in one durative sentence reaching to their deaths, outside the Sheba pursuit's event line, on the single-verse notice standard (11:1; 17:23). The notice's isolation is doubled in the layout, a setumah closing it at 20:3 (single-witness).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the notice into the homecoming frame of the Amasa commission — rejected because 20:4 opens a new command scene with a speech formula ('Then the king said to Amasa, Call me the men of Judah') on the revolt's event line, while 20:3 is lifetime-scope household chronography: the registers do not mix, and the notice's function is retrospective closure, not scene-setting.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (Amasa's commission, delay, and the Abishai dispatch)
boundary_rationale: The command formula 'Then the king said to Amasa, Call me the men of Judah together within three days' (web:2Sam.20.4) opens the mobilization unit: Amasa's overdue delay notice (web:2Sam.20.5), and the emergency re-dispatch to Abishai with the threat assessment 'Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom did' (web:2Sam.20.6) — commission, failure, and replacement dispatch forming one command-chain sequence that quietly sets Amasa on the collision course with Joab. A closed interval separates delay from re-dispatch in the codex (after 20:5, single-witness); inside one mobilization crisis it registers a beat, not a boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the Abishai dispatch 20:6 as its own unit — rejected because the dispatch is the immediate remedial response to 20:5's delay within one continuous mobilization crisis (the three-day clock set at 20:4 governs all three verses); severing failure from remedy would break the causal spine that explains why two commanders converge at Gibeon.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (the murder of Amasa at the great stone)
boundary_rationale: The pursuit departure 'Joab's men went out after him with the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men' (web:2Sam.20.7) opens the Gibeon scene: the great-stone meeting with the narrator's sword-apparatus staging ('as he went along it fell out', web:2Sam.20.8), the kiss-greeting 'Is it well with you, my brother?' with the beard-grip (web:2Sam.20.9), the unheeded sword and the single disemboweling stroke (web:2Sam.20.10), the rally cry 'He who favors Joab, and he who is for David, let him follow Joab!' (web:2Sam.20.11), and the wallowing-corpse removal with the resumed pursuit close 'all the people went on after Joab to pursue Sheba' (web:2Sam.20.12-13) — deed and its traffic management in one location-bound scene. The murder scene carries two internal samekh spaces (20:8, 20:10, single-witness); the great stone holds one continuous action regardless of how the scribes breathed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the corpse-removal 20:11-13 from the murder — rejected because the removal happens at the same highway spot as an immediate consequence (the army halting at the body is the murder's direct effect, resolved by the garment-covering), and the pursuit-resumption notice at 20:13 is the scene's designed close, returning the column to the Sheba chase.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (siege of Abel of Beth Maacah)
boundary_rationale: Sheba's itinerary formula 'He went through all the tribes of Israel to Abel, to Beth Maacah' with the Berites' rally (web:2Sam.20.14) shifts the narrative to the fugitive's terminus, and the siege notice — the mound cast up against the rampart and all Joab's people battering the wall (web:2Sam.20.15) — sets the crisis the wise woman's negotiation resolves; itinerary and investment form the compact military frame of the closing scene.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Fusing the siege with the negotiation 20:16-22 — rejected because 20:16 opens with the wise woman's cry formula ('Then a wise woman cried out of the city, Hear, hear!') introducing a new speaking participant and switching mode from siege-works narration to parley dialogue; the wall is the literal boundary the dialogue crosses.

literature_type_guess: narrative_dialogue (the wise woman of Abel's negotiation)
boundary_rationale: The cry formula 'Then a wise woman cried out of the city, Hear, hear! Please say to Joab, Come near here' (web:2Sam.20.16) opens the parley: the are-you-Joab identification exchange (web:2Sam.20.17), the ask-counsel-at-Abel proverb with the mother-in-Israel and Yahweh's-inheritance appeal (web:2Sam.20.18-19), Joab's far-be-it disavowal narrowing the demand to one man (web:2Sam.20.20-21), the head-over-the-wall pledge, and the execution close — Sheba beheaded, the trumpet dispersal 'every man to his tent', and Joab's return to Jerusalem to the king (web:2Sam.20.22) — negotiation and settlement completing the revolt narrative on the same trumpet-signal instrument that opened it (20:1). As Joab turns back to Jerusalem the codex closes a section too (setumah after 20:22, single-witness), agreement of the lightest kind.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the execution 20:22 from the parley — rejected because 20:22's beheading is the immediate performance of the woman's 20:21 pledge in one continuous siege-resolution (she goes from the wall-top exchange directly to the people 'in her wisdom'), and the trumpet-and-return close is the negotiation's outcome, not a new scene; pledge and payment belong together per the command-execution pattern.

boundary_rationale: A formal officer register with a varied prepositional/appositional mixture, not a fixed formula, matching the pattern documented at the parallel register in 8:15-18 (M8-2Sam-048) -- MT's own preposition for Joab is אֶל rather than עַל (oshb:2Sam.20.23, וְיוֹאָב אֶל כָּל הַצָּבָא יִשְׂרָאֵל, WEB 'was over all the army of Israel'), while Benaiah's clause does take עַל ('Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and over the Pelethites', web:2Sam.20.23 / oshb:2Sam.20.23), Adoram over the forced labor and Jehoshaphat recorder (web:2Sam.20.24), Sheva scribe, and 'Zadok and Abiathar were כֹּהֲנִים (priests)' (web:2Sam.20.25 / oshb:2Sam.20.25), and 'Ira the Jairite was also כֹהֵן (WEB: chief minister) to David' (web:2Sam.20.26 / oshb:2Sam.20.26) -- the second recension of the 8:15-18 register, forming with it a structural bracket around the whole court narrative (chs 9-20) -- a cross-span pairing disclosed here as thematic framing rather than claimed as a boundary-driving inclusio for this span, since only this row's own span (20:23-26) lies within the decision being made. Rendering כֹהֵן/כֹהֲנִים consistently across both verses, rather than following WEB's split rendering 'priests'/'chief minister,' makes the register's central delta visible rather than concealing it: the office named כהן is precisely what varies between the two recensions, since 8:18's parallel clause reads וּבְנֵי דָוִד כֹּהֲנִים הָיוּ ('David's sons were כֹּהֲנִים'), replaced here by Ira. Its other notable delta -- Adoram's forced-labor portfolio, absent from 8:15-18 -- is a content variation inside the same register genre. The register's final entry is trailed by the manuscript's own terminal spacing (setumah at 20:26, single-witness), list and layout ending in step.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the register to the Sheba resolution as its aftermath -- rejected because the register is durative administrative chronography with no event-line connection to the siege (Joab's return at 20:22 already closed the revolt): the list's genre, formula, and bracketing function with 8:15-18 mark it as a freestanding register unit per the list-register rule.

boundary_rationale: A single-verse arc-opening frame — 'There was a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year; and David sought the face of Yahweh' with the quoted oracle 'It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he put the Gibeonites to death' (web:2Sam.21.1) — durative chronography plus divine diagnosis, establishing cause and culprit for the whole 21:1-14 arc, on the single-verse frame standard of 3:1 and 11:1. Its self-containment is reflected by a samekh space after 21:1 (single-witness; a Prophets parashah, hence weak-tier at best).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Heading the Gibeonite negotiation with 21:1 — rejected because 21:2 re-enters scene time with a summons formula ('The king called the Gibeonites and said to them') plus the narrator's Amorite-remnant parenthesis, while 21:1 spans three years and contains the arc's divine warrant: frame and scene are register-distinct, and the frame governs the burial resolution at 21:14 as much as the negotiation.

boundary_rationale: The summons formula 'The king called the Gibeonites and said to them' with the narrator's identity parenthesis (web:2Sam.21.2) opens the negotiation: David's what-should-I-do atonement question (web:2Sam.21.3), the Gibeonites' no-silver-or-gold demurral with David's blank-check reply (web:2Sam.21.4), the seven-sons demand 'we will hang them up to Yahweh in Gibeah of Saul' (web:2Sam.21.5-6), and the royal grant 'I will give them' closing the exchange. Between grant speech and handover the codex leaves a closed interval (after 21:6, single-witness), where the disposition's own exception notice makes the real cut.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending through the handover 21:7-9 -- rejected because 21:7 opens a new movement from negotiated terms to their selective execution: 'the king spared Mephibosheth... because of Yahweh's oath' translates a plain narrative wayyiqtol, וַיַּחְמֹל הַמֶּלֶךְ עַל מְפִיבֹשֶׁת (oshb:2Sam.21.7), not a disjunctive -- nothing is fronted before the verb and no adversative particle is present, so WEB's 'But' supplies a contrast the Hebrew syntax does not mark. The seam still holds on content grounds: the negotiation closes on the grant speech ('I will give them,' 21:6), and 21:7-9's wayyiqtol chain narrates the enacted disposition -- sparing, naming, handing over, hanging -- which is a register shift from dialogue to narrated action regardless of the syntactic label.

boundary_rationale: The exception notice opens the execution unit on a plain narrative wayyiqtol, not a disjunctive: 21:7 reads וַיַּחְמֹל הַמֶּלֶךְ עַל מְפִיבֹשֶׁת בֶּן יְהוֹנָתָן בֶּן שָׁאוּל עַל שְׁבֻעַת יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר בֵּינֹתָם ('the king spared Mephibosheth... because of Yahweh's oath that was between them') -- verb-initial, with no fronted constituent and no adversative particle, so WEB's 'But' is the translator's connective rather than Hebrew syntax; the register shift from negotiated terms (21:2-6) to enacted disposition is carried instead by the wayyiqtol narrative chain that runs from sparing through naming, handover, and hanging. The naming of the seven taken follows at 21:8 -- Rizpah's two sons (אֶת שְׁנֵי בְּנֵי רִצְפָּה בַת אַיָּה, Armoni and Mephibosheth) and five more sons of Saul's daughter, whom MT names מִיכַל ('Michal'), אֲשֶׁר יָלְדָה לְעַדְרִיאֵל בֶּן בַּרְזִלַּי הַמְּחֹלָתִי -- with no ketiv/qere variant at this verse. This substrate's own witness names Michal, not Merab; WEB's 'Merab' is a translator harmonization resolving the tension between this verse and 2Sam.6:23 ('Michal... had no child') by borrowing the Adriel marriage from 1Sam.18:19, where the bride is Merab -- a resolution reached elsewhere in the Samuel corpus, not via Chronicles. That harmonization is disclosed here as a known crux rather than presented as MT's own reading. The handover and hanging follow at 21:9, 'on the mountain before Yahweh,' with a genuinely double calendar clause -- בִּימֵי קָצִיר בָּרִאשֹׁנִים followed by בִּתְחִלַּת קְצִיר שְׂעֹרִים, 'in the first days, at the beginning of barley harvest' -- which both closes the deed and opens the vigil's clock at 21:10 (מִתְּחִלַּת קָצִיר).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Fusing the handover with Rizpah's vigil 21:10 -- rejected because 21:10 changes acting subject and register entirely (from royal disposition to one bereaved mother's months-long sackcloth watch, durative 'from the beginning of harvest until water poured on them'): deed and vigil are separate movements, seamed at the subject change.

literature_type_guess: narrative_prose (Rizpah's vigil and the burial of Saul's bones)
boundary_rationale: The subject-change notice 'Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock' with its durative bird-and-beast watch (web:2Sam.21.10) opens the resolution arc: the report to David (21:11), the retrieval of Saul's and Jonathan's bones from Jabesh Gilead with the narrator's Beth Shan retrospect (web:2Sam.21.12-13), the gathering of the hanged men's bones, and the burial in Kish's tomb at Zela closing on the theological seal 'After that, God answered prayer for the land' (web:2Sam.21.14) — the famine frame of 21:1 resolved, an inclusio the appendix repeats at 24:25. The answered-prayer seal has a scribal counterpart, an open division after 21:14 (single-witness) — the famine arc closed on both levels at once.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the bone-retrieval 21:12-14 from the vigil 21:10-11 — rejected because the report verse explicitly makes the vigil the retrieval's cause ('David was told what Rizpah… had done', 21:11) in one continuous causal chain from watch to burial to answered prayer; severing cause from effect would orphan both halves of the arc's resolution.

boundary_rationale: The campaign formula 'The Philistines had war again with Israel' (web:2Sam.21.15) opens a four-vignette register bound by the iterative war-formula chain (וַתְּהִי עוֹד + מִלְחָמָה, 'there was again war' -- articular הַמִּלְחָמָה at 21:18/21:19, anarthrous מִלְחָמָה at 21:15/21:20 -- four occurrences matching the four vignettes): the Ishbibenob rescue with the lamp-of-Israel oath (web:2Sam.21.16-17), Sibbecai's Saph (21:18), Elhanan's exploit against Goliath with the weaver's-beam spear (21:19), and the six-fingered champion of Gath (21:20-21), closed by the summarizing count 'These four were born to the giant in Gath; and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants' (web:2Sam.21.22) -- a formula that explicitly totals all four vignettes into one register. On the third vignette: MT 21:19 names the victim plainly, אֵת גָּלְיָת הַגִּתִּי ('Goliath the Gittite'), with no אָח ('brother') and no ketiv/qere variant; the campaign's WEB source text nonetheless prints 'Goliath the Gittite's brother,' a harmonization toward 1 Chronicles 20:5 that is disclosed here rather than adopted as MT's own reading, on the same principle applied to the 14:27/18:18 son-count tension. This divergence does not touch the register's boundary, since neither edge depends on the disputed word: the iterative war-formula opens each vignette and the summary count at 21:22 closes all four regardless of which name is read at 21:19. Inside the chain the codex spaces the vignette joints themselves — open breaks at 21:17 and 21:18, a closed one at 21:19, all single-witness — scribal footsteps following the formula, while the register's own summary binds the four into one.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the first vignette 21:15-17 (with its lamp-of-Israel oath and real narrative development) from the formulaic chain 21:18-22 -- rejected because the closing count 'These four' at 21:22 ranges over all four giants including Ishbibenob: the register's own summary formula forbids severing its first member, and per the list-register rule narrative insets (like Benaiah's exploits in 23:20-23) live inside their register; the oath is disclosed as the register's largest inset.

boundary_rationale: A formal psalm superscription — 'David spoke to Yahweh the words of this song in the day that Yahweh delivered him out of the hand of all his enemies, and out of the hand of Saul, and he said' (web:2Sam.22.1-2) — frames the entire chapter as one quoted composition (the substrate's q1/q2 poetry markers run unbroken from 22:2 to 22:51): rock-fortress invocation (web:2Sam.22.2-4), death-waters distress and theophany (22:5-20), righteousness recital (22:21-28), military empowerment (22:29-46), and the closing doxology 'Yahweh lives!… He gives great deliverance to his king, and shows loving kindness to his anointed, to David and to his offspring, forever more' (web:2Sam.22.47-51) — whose anointed-offspring cadence answers the superscription's deliverance claim as a designed inclusio. After the doxology's last line the manuscript opens a new parashah (petuchah at 22:51, single-witness), the layout bowing out with the song. The unit is chapter-shaped by literary warrant (one superscribed song ‖ Ps 18), not by chapter-fallback.
